#5169. Hyperscalers List GPUs at Nearly 2× the GPU-Cloud Price, Fluence Research Finds

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

The AI Compute Race report prices GPU compute outside the biggest buyers: a three-year commitment cuts the median price by 48%, while 17 of 22 tracked GPU models rose in price over the past year

DALLAS, Texas – November 13, 2026 – Fluence has published The AI Compute Race, a report that prices GPU cloud compute for every company that is not a frontier lab or a hyperscaler. It was produced with research partners NEAR AI, io.net, Boundless, Phala, Gensyn, Fortytwo, Theta, Compute Labs and GAIB. Its central finding: where a company buys a GPU-hour sets the price. Across H100, H200 and B200 models, hyperscalers list GPUs at 1.98 times the GPU-cloud median, from 1.4 times on the B200 to 2.8 times on the H100. The same H200 lists from $4.08 to $10.60 an hour.

Commitment length matters almost as much as provider choice. Against each provider’s own on-demand rate, a one-year reservation cuts the median price by 21% and a three-year term by 48%. Spot capacity lists at 53% of on-demand, for workloads that can be interrupted.

Buyers who expect GPU prices to fall may need to recheck their budgets. Seventeen of the 22 GPU models tracked by GetDeploying cost more than a year earlier, and the median H100 rents for 13% to 30% more, depending on the window measured.

The report also traces why prices are rapidly rising:

“Open-weight models are close behind the best closed ones, and companies are switching to them. Any company with GPUs can now serve a near-frontier model on hardware it controls. The GPUs are the hard part,” said Evgeny Ponomarev, Co-founder of Fluence.

The report closes with four ways to pay less for the same compute: compare the same chip across provider types, commit when the workload is steady, match the GPU generation to the model, and look beyond the hyperscalers, since much of the newest neocloud capacity is contracted to labs years ahead.

The full report is available at fluence.ai/compute-race-2026.

Fluence Cloud is a GPU cloud provider with capacity from independent data centers (fluence.ai). Founded in 2017 by Dmitry Kurinskiy, Evgeny Ponomarev and Tom Trowbridge, the company has raised $14 million from investors including 1KX, Multicoin, Distributed Global, Blockchange, Tiger Global and Protocol Labs.

#5168. How TSMC’s employee data leak raises questions over cloud security

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) confirmed on the 12th of November that some current and former employees’ personal information had appeared online without authorization.

As per reports, the hacker has asked for 3 BTC, which is worth about $220K, for a database they claimed held 46,000 employee records. The hackers claimed to have 6.9 GB of data and threatened to publish it within a week without a buyer. However, no payment has been publicly verified, as of press time.

For the unaware, TSMC makes chips for other companies. They said that the leaked records matched data held by a cloud provider. Notably, these records included names, national ID numbers, and banking details, according to Taiwan News.

The company’s own review found no evidence of a break in its systems. As of the latest update from the company, they were notifying affected staff and working with the cloud provider and investigators.

Looking at the impact this news had, TSMC’s U.S. listed shares opened 4.53% lower at $394.62 on the 12th of November. They recovered some ground to close at $405.49, down 1.90% on the day. By the way, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) followed a similar path, opening 4.33% lower and ending the session down 1.03%.

With chip stocks also under pressure, it was difficult to tell how much of TSMC’s drop was due to the leak.

Needless to say, this leak surfaced before a volatile session for chipmakers and AI cloud providers. The semiconductor ETF recovered much of its early loss, even though the individual chip stocks went in different directions.

Notably, Nvidia fell 4.34% after announcing CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. On the other hand, AMD and Broadcom both gained, rising 5.86% and 5.54%, respectively.

Furthermore, the Kobeissi Letter identified intraday losses in Nebius, CoreWeave, and IREN.

TSMC’s annual filing says it sets security or confidentiality requirements for outside providers. Going back to 2023, it cut off data exchange with supplier Kinmax after a breach exposed server setup information.

That vendor connection actually raises liability questions that don’t get enough attention in breach discussions

Another user shared a different perspective,

Your employer picked the vendor. you just get the breach notice

The type of employee data matters for a different reason. Binance said its October theft followed a campaign that targeted engineers before reaching its wallet signing service.

Furthermore, the ransom of 3 Bitcoin [BTC] puts the listing in the context of a wider trade in stolen data. Moreover, Chainalysis tracked $87.5 million in on-chain volume at fraud shops in 2025.

#5166. New US report reveals yen rescue used euros, not dollars. That matters for Bitcoin

The November 12 report confirms that Treasury used euro reserves to buy yen on July 31, not newly created Fed dollars.

The US Treasury financed July’s yen intervention with euros from its reserves, the New York Fed confirmed in a November 12 report. For Bitcoin, the funding currency limits the operation’s significance as a signal of fresh Federal Reserve dollar liquidity.

On July 31, the New York Fed bought 79.4 billion yen in the spot market against euro sales from Treasury’s Exchange Stabilization Fund, or ESF. The aim was to counter what Treasury viewed as disorderly yen moves.

The New York Fed executed the trade as Treasury’s fiscal agent. The Federal Reserve itself did not intervene in foreign-exchange markets during the third quarter. Treasury’s ESF operating framework identifies yen and euros as its foreign-currency assets and describes the New York Fed’s trading role. An exchange of those reserve currencies alone supplies no evidence of new Fed dollars entering Bitcoin markets.

A separate mechanism does provide dollar funding abroad: central-bank dollar liquidity swaps. Under those arrangements, the Fed exchanges dollars for a foreign central bank’s currency, with an agreement to reverse the transaction.

The report shows less borrowing outstanding through that facility at quarter-end. Aggregate balances fell from $250 million on June 30 to $207 million on September 30, 2026. The Bank of Japan had none outstanding at September’s end; the remaining balances were with the European Central Bank and Bank of England.

Offshore dollar funding conditions were stable during Q3, the report says, with generally low borrowing premiums in major currency pairs. Those quarter-end stocks do not measure gross lending during the quarter or establish November’s funding conditions.

The July trade used Treasury euros. A Fed dollar swap is a different funding route.

July 31 operation, disclosed November 12: the New York Fed traded ESF euros for 79.4 billion yen on Treasury’s behalf.

Facility mechanics only: dollars are exchanged for a foreign central bank’s currency, with a binding reversal.

This euro-funded trade does not establish new Fed dollars for Bitcoin. Leverage remains a possible spillover channel.

July 31 operation and November 12 disclosure are distinct. The swap option explains a facility, not a newly observed transaction. Neither route identifies Bitcoin purchases or current yen-funded deleveraging.

Source-bound chronology and directional currency-exchange diagrams. Arrows show the currency exchanged, not flow size. Dates are sequence markers, not a scaled timeline. No original calculation or inferred market flow.

July 31 operation and November 12 disclosure are distinct. The swap option explains a facility, not a newly observed transaction. Neither route identifies Bitcoin purchases or current yen-funded deleveraging.

The more recent BOJ exchange-rate sheet recorded dollar/yen at 159.70–71 at 17:00 JST on November 12. That is a dated market observation, not an announced intervention threshold.

Bitcoin’s potential exposure runs through leverage. A stronger yen makes unhedged yen borrowing more expensive to repay in another currency. If volatility raises margin demands, leveraged investors may need to raise cash or cut positions, spreading pressure beyond the original currency trade.

Research by the Bank for International Settlements found that leveraged equity and currency unwinds amplified August 2024’s market shock, with margin increases and further reductions in leverage worsening volatility. Crypto also responds to wider financial conditions: IMF working-paper authors found that US monetary tightening reduced a broad crypto price factor through investors’ appetite for risk.

These mechanisms explain how a yen-funded unwind could pressure Bitcoin, but the report does not establish current Bitcoin flows or a present unwind. July’s euro-funded yen intervention is not evidence of new Fed dollars entering crypto.

#5165. Strategy Sends Crucial Message on Bitcoin's Quantum Security

Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, has sent an important message regarding Bitcoin’s future resistance to quantum computing attacks.

The company, which was co-founded by renowned Bitcoin champion Michael Saylor, recently posted on X that the Bitcoin network can implement new security measures as and when they are needed.

“Quantum-resistant upgrades can be adopted if & when it's needed,” wrote Strategy.

These comments come at a time when the crypto industry is debating whether the rise of quantum computing could, in the long run, threaten Bitcoin’s cryptographic security.

Given that Bitcoin leverages elliptic curve cryptography for transaction security, quantum computing could pose a significant threat to Bitcoin.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer has the potential to reverse-engineer private keys from exposed public keys. This could give attackers access to the Bitcoin holdings associated with those keys.

At this point, there is no known publicly available quantum computer that can successfully break Bitcoin’s cryptography in this manner.

While speaking at the World Bank in Washington in October, Saylor said that the Bitcoin network would be able to defend itself against any realistic quantum computing threat by coming together and upgrading the software.

Saylor estimated that such an upgrade would take about 90 days once a worldwide consensus is reached on the need for quantum-resistant cryptography.

Saylor also warned against the hasty introduction of new cryptography. He reasoned that more complex security measures may themselves introduce weaknesses.

However, the 90-day estimate has come under scrutiny because such a network-wide shift would involve developers agreeing on technical changes and Bitcoin users moving their funds to new, secure addresses.

Interestingly, Strategy has also initiated efforts aimed at research and development for Bitcoin’s long-term security.

In July, Strategy was part of a group of seven major financial institutions and crypto companies, including BlackRock and Coinbase, that formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium.

The Bitcoin Security Consortium has committed $15 million over three years. One of the areas of focus of the consortium is post-quantum cryptography.

In fact, Bitcoin developers are already working on ways to address the quantum computing issue.

One of the most prominent proposals is Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360 (BIP-360). This BIP introduces a new type of transaction output, Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR).

#5164. DOJ Wins Court Authority to Seize $1.2 Billion of North Korea’s Stolen Binance Crypto as Freezes Top $2.7 Billion

The DOJ said Thursday it has court authority to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, part of a freeze of more than $2.7 billion that officials said halted about half of North Korea’s October exchange heist.

In a Thursday announcement, the department said that on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as TraderTraitor, stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from Binance. That is below the $6.34 billion figure Binance has covered since the attack.

Binance said it had completed coverage of the assets hit in the breach, replacing the tokens from company funds rather than by recovering the stolen coins. Those are separate tracks: the DOJ is trying to interdict what was taken, while the exchange has said users were made whole from its Secure Asset Fund for Users, a portion of its futures insurance fund and its treasury.

Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ’s Criminal Division said the department and its partners were able to “immediately halt about half of this historic breach” by freezing stolen assets “before they got beyond law enforcement reach.” The freeze of more than $2.7 billion is a joint figure for U.S. government and private-sector efforts. Of that amount, the DOJ said it has already obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion. The underlying court papers were not posted with the announcement.

The $1.2 billion is not newly recovered money but comes out of the roughly $2.85 billion Binance said on Nov. 3 had been frozen or intercepted, and Thursday’s court authorization is the legal step that lets the government move toward taking ownership of those funds through forfeiture, where until now they had simply been frozen at the token issuers.

Even that freeze is not the end of the trail. The DOJ said TraderTraitor actors are still moving the stolen assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges, and that tracing, seizure and forfeiture work continues. Last week, on Oct. 31, the FBI, with the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft to North Korea and urging virtual asset service providers to block transactions with or derived from addresses the actors are using. The alert said investigators have seen the stolen assets converted primarily into ether.

Separately from the DOJ and Binance case, the U.S. attorney’s office in the Central District of California and the FBI announced the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in a social engineering campaign the FBI is calling FaceStealer. The FBI said the scheme has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the last 18 months and has also been used in attempts to compromise people who maintain open-source software, a step the bureau said appears calculated to enable supply-chain attacks.

The method is a fake video call. The FBI said North Korean hackers, known publicly under names including APT38 and BlueNoroff, lure targets with meeting invitations sent from accounts stolen from earlier victims. Once a target joins, the hackers play a prerecorded webcam video of a person the target knows, or a deepfake of a well-known figure in the cryptocurrency industry, then introduce a fake technical error and send a “fix” that installs malware. In several cases, the theft came months to more than a year after the first compromise, as the hackers waited for wallet balances to grow.

A Thursday FBI FLASH report said the meetings run on imposter versions of Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet, with invitations often moving through hijacked Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack or Discord accounts. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims. The bureau has posted a hub for the campaign at fbi.gov/facestealer.

Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor tied both Thursday’s actions to the same charge: “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft.”

The Binance recovery is still being run by the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division and Virtual Asset Unit, with the Secret Service and IRS-CI. The DOJ did not say how much of the more than $2.7 billion freeze, or of the $1.2 billion under court authority, is bitcoin.

#5160. Digital Credit: Comparing The Six Bitcoin Preferred Stocks

A simple four-part investor framework for evaluating Digital Credit.

Digital credit is an emerging asset class that transforms corporate Bitcoin balance sheets into income producing securities. Strategy pioneered the market with five perpetual preferred equity instruments: STRK, STRF, STRD, STRC, and STRE (the first four are listed in the U.S.). Strive subsequently introduced SATA and SATS, bringing the category to six U.S. instruments across two issuers.

These securities offer investors preferred equity (read: credit-like) exposure to companies whose balance sheets are dominated by Bitcoin. Their perpetual structure means investors principally rely on recurring dividends and the continued financial strength of the issuer. Unlike term debt, there is no maturation date at which the full principal is ever paid back.

Evaluating digital credit requires examining four characteristics: creditworthiness, investor protections, liquidity, and dividend profile.

This article explains all four dimensions and then offers a ranking for the six digital credit instruments along these lines. None of this should be taken as investment advice—it is only a systematic framework for analyzing digital credit.

Creditworthiness measures an issuer’s ability to support its financial obligations.

Traditional credit analysis focuses on earnings, free cash flow, and refinancing capacity. Companies with strong cash generation can service interest and repay maturing debt. Digital credit issuers today derive financial strength primarily from their Bitcoin reserves, placing greater emphasis on net asset coverage. In the future we could certainly see digital credit issuers that also have significant cash flows on top of Bitcoin holdings, which would add to creditworthiness.

The central question is how much Bitcoin supports each dollar of credit obligations. One useful measure is the BTC Rating, which compares the dollar value of Bitcoin reserves with the outstanding credit, accounting for the seniority of each credit instrument. Cash reserves can further strengthen creditworthiness by reducing net obligations.

For example, a 5x BTC Rating indicates five dollars of Bitcoin supporting every dollar of notional credit claims. Higher ratings provide greater protection against Bitcoin price declines.

Seniority matters because instruments from the same issuer can have different claims on the same asset base. A senior preferred instrument benefits from greater coverage than a junior preferred instrument: all senior claims are included in the BTC Rating calculation of a junior instrument.

Creditworthiness also depends on corporate governance and capital allocation. Management must preserve sufficient Bitcoin coverage while funding recurring dividends. Issuing additional credit increases dividend obligations, while assets accumulation (Bitcoin or cash) strengthen the asset base. Excessive leverage, poor treasury management, or sustained Bitcoin declines can weaken coverage over time.

Investors must therefore evaluate both their assumptions about Bitcoin’s long term performance and management’s ability to maintain a sustainable capital structure.

Investor protections determine what happens when an issuer fails to pay its promised dividends.

While creditworthiness concerns an issuer’s ability to pay, investor protections govern the consequences of missed payments, and more specifically the compensation investors may receive for delayed income.

The first distinction is cumulative versus noncumulative dividends. Cumulative dividends continue accumulating when payments are skipped, preserving the investor’s claim to unpaid distributions. Noncumulative dividends permit the issuer to permanently forgo a payment.

The second distinction is the treatment of unpaid dividends. Some instruments preserve unpaid amounts without additional compensation. Others compound arrears at the regular dividend rate. The strongest protections impose penalty rates, which cause unpaid dividends to compound at progressively higher rates as deferrals continue.

Penalty rates create financial incentives for management to maintain regular payments. They also compensate investors for the additional risk and delay associated with missed distributions.

Other investor protections may include restrictions on payments to junior shareholders, preferred shareholder voting rights or director elections, and dedicated dividend reserves.

These provisions establish the contractual guardrails surrounding dividend payments. Stronger protections increase the cost of deferral and improve the investor’s position to receive income.

Liquidity measures how easily investors can enter and exit positions without materially affecting market prices. This is especially important for digital credit, which does not mature and pay back principal on a fixed date. A liquid market is how an investor would “get his money back” if he wants to exit his position.

Digital credit has developed substantial secondary market liquidity, particularly in its leading instruments. The six U.S.-listed digital credit tickers are among the most actively traded preferred equity securities in the U.S. markets.

Two metrics help investors evaluate liquidity.

Absolute trading volume measures the total dollar value traded over a given period. Greater volume accommodates larger transactions and makes it easier for institutions to establish or liquidate positions.

Relative liquidity, or turnover, measures trading volume as a percentage of an instrument’s market capitalization. It captures how actively a security trades relative to its outstanding size.

For example, an instrument with $50 million in daily volume and a $1 billion market capitalization has 5% daily turnover. Another instrument trading $100 million daily with a $10 billion market capitalization has only 1% turnover. The second instrument offers greater absolute trading capacity, while the first experiences substantially greater trading activity relative to its size.

Absolute volume facilitates large transactions, while relative turnover reveals the level of trading activity relative to the capital outstanding.

Dividend profile describes the characteristics of the income an investor receives. Three main considerations are the dividend rate policy, payment frequency, and dividend yield.

The first distinction is between fixed and variable dividends. Fixed dividends establish a predetermined annual payment per share. Investors know the nominal income they are entitled to receive, allowing them to plan around a predictable cash flow stream. Variable dividends allow issuers to adjust the payout rate over time. These adjustments can respond to market interest rates, investor demand, or the trading price of the instrument. Fixed dividends prioritize income predictability for investors with reduced flexibility for issuers. Variable dividends provide flexibility for issuers but less predictability for investors.

The second consideration is payment frequency. Traditional preferred securities generally pay quarterly. Digital credit has introduced monthly, twice monthly, and daily dividend schedules. More frequent payments improve cash flow availability, accelerate reinvestment opportunities, and reduce the concentration of distributions around individual payment dates. After January 1 2027, all six instruments will be doing daily dividends.

The third consideration, and perhaps the most important out of anything mentioned in this article, is the raw dividend yield. This is the annualized income received divided by the trading price of the credit. A higher yield is generally preferred, but it also must be contextualized against risks and other considerations.

The following framework ranks the six instruments relative to one another. Rank 1 represents the strongest position and rank 6 the weakest, with ties where instruments share identical characteristics.

Creditworthiness and investor protections receive overall rankings. Liquidity is segmented into absolute trading volume and turnover. Dividend profile is segmented into rate certainty and yield. While each category’s segments can be evaluated together as a composite metric based on the investor’s own needs, I am choosing to segment them for more precision. I have also thrown out payment frequency since all six will be daily in less than two months.

For dividend rate certainty, fixed dividends rank ahead of variable dividends because their nominal payments are predetermined. This ranking specifically measures income predictability.

Equal signs indicate tied rankings. Liquidity rankings are based on average daily trading volumes from November 2–11, 2026, and turnover is calculated using the latest reported shares outstanding.

Creditworthiness: Strategy’s preferreds rank ahead of Strive’s because of their greater asset coverage. Within each issuer, seniority determines the ranking. STRF has the highest BTC Rating because it is Strategy’s most senior preferred, while SATS has the lowest coverage because it ranks below SATA in Strive’s capital structure.

Investor protections: SATA and STRF rank first and second because unpaid dividends compound at escalating penalty rates and holders can elect directors following prolonged dividend deferrals. SATA’s higher penalty rate ceiling and dividend reserve give it the edge. STRC and STRK both compound unpaid dividends at the regular dividend rate. I rank STRC ahead of STRK based on its higher current compounding rate, although STRK also gives holders the right to elect directors after prolonged dividend deferrals. SATS has cumulative dividends, but unpaid dividends do not compound. STRD ranks last because its dividends are noncumulative, meaning any skipped dividends are permanently forgone. Investors also have no right to bring on directors.

Of the six, STRC and SATA are variable rate instruments and the remaining four are fixed rate. This makes the dividend rate policy pretty straightforward.

The remaining columns—volume, turnover, and yield—are trackable numbers. For instance, here are turnover and volume numbers from the BFC Digital Credit Dashboard:

Each of the six digital credit instruments has a different set of tradeoffs. Investors who prioritize creditworthiness may prefer STRF, while those who prioritize dividend certainty and yield may prefer SATS.

The relative importance of each of these dimensions depends on the investor’s own needs. As digital credit continues to develop, investors can use this framework to evaluate new instruments and determine which ones are best suited to their objectives.

#5159. This Guy Lost 54 Pounds and Got Absolutely Shredded in 6 Months

At 46, Austin Cowburn wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

At age 46, Austin Cowburn felt his training was "directionless," and he started putting on weight. This former runner and marathoner wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

RUNNING HAS ALWAYS been my go-to exercise; as a younger man I joined several running clubs, and even finished as even finished pretty high up in the 1995 New York Marathon. I spent weeknights and Saturday mornings on the track or in a swimming pool. Cardio is familiar to me, and as I grew up, I stuck with it. Looking back, I realize means I didn’t have the understanding and technique to really benefit from weight training.

After a couple of years of directionless training, plus two injuries and rehab, and a poor diet, I put on weight. That inflamed other, niggling injuries, which made me feel like I just wasn’t at my best. I felt sluggish; my favorite clothes didn’t fit as well, and the new ones seemed to be smaller than I expected. I wanted to get back into marathons, but to do that I need to get fitter, stronger, and healthier. So, I approached Ultimate Performance Manchester for help.

We started with fundamental stuff: monitoring and being consistent with my diet. I went from eating a lot of rich, calorie-laden food, eating it at all times of the day, to something much more sustainable. I’d enjoy a blended berry smoothie in the morning with protein, and three scrambled eggs with spinach in mid-morning. Mid-afternoon and evening, I’d eat lean-meat chili, mainly turkey mince, with lots of vegetables thrown in, including peppers and tomatoes, as well as rice. I also enjoyed a low-fat, high-protein yogurt in the evening mixed with banana, honey, or chia seeds. On the weekend, I could indulge in a nice steak.

We often forget how big an impact diet can have on mood, energy levels, and your ability to train hard and get the best from yourself. Changing what I ate really reminded me of the importance of a foundational diet.

I trained three times a week in the gym, usually from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. I loved getting it done first thing in the morning, which really set me up for the day. I would also run four times a week. I really got my love for running back during this time: my distances increased, and I had no injuries. I didn’t even have aches and pains afterward. Training, losing weight, and fueling my body correctly really helped me regain my fluidity of motion.

It also helped with my energy levels and sleep. I felt mentally sharper, more productive and more creative. People told me that my skin was glowing. Everyone was extremely positive and kind in and out of the gym, complimentary, and really encouraging. My family was very proud and surprised with the results, and I felt like the very best version of myself.

In six months, I lost 24.6 kg (54 pounds), bringing my body fat percentage from 28.2% to 11.6%. I dropped from an extra-large to a medium. I’ve continued training, and now I’m eating more, and building muscle mass. I’m looking to sustain my gains and also increase the number of exercises I have in my toolbox.

It’s great to be able to say that more, better training has helped me avoid injuries. The more I trained, the more I wanted to, and my stamina has gone through the roof. I’m happier, more relaxed, and more motivated; I just feel better about myself.

I think anyone can do this, and if you’re on the fence about it, just go for it. Set clear goals and look for help, whether that’s a professional trainer or just a friend who’ll hold you accountable. You don’t have to change all at once; I’d recommend not putting too much pressure on yourself from session to session. Enjoy your exercises; make sure you rest and refuel correctly.

#5157. Amazon says no human wrote or reviewed the code for its new cloud testing tool

Human engineers designed the guardrails and release checks. Application security still needs testing on the real cloud.

Amazon released AWS Emulator on Nov. 11, a local tool that imitates AWS services so developers can test cloud applications on their own machines. The company says autonomous AI agents wrote and reviewed its implementation.

In Amazon's engineering account, engineer Matthew Goldberg says his team neither wrote nor reviewed the emulator code. He also describes the substantial engineering work needed to turn an experiment into a product, including the guardrails and checks that determine which changes can ship.

Amazon describes three teams of agents: one manages fidelity tests, another finds differences between the emulator and real AWS, and a third fixes individual issues. Changes face checks for compilation, coding standards, security and regressions before merging, according to the company.

The test agents work from public AWS API models and verify their scenarios against the real cloud. The public evaluation suite says every fidelity test was checked against at least two sandboxed AWS accounts.

AWS calls the degree of agreement with its cloud services “fidelity.” A test passes when the emulator matches AWS for every call in that workflow, including status codes, resulting resources, side effects and errors, according to its fidelity documentation. Returning success where AWS returns an error fails that test.

The boundary is coverage. The evaluation repository explicitly says behavior without a fidelity test is unverified. Passing a scenario establishes a match for that scenario; it does not establish that every way an application uses AWS will work.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

AWS defines a pass within a tested workflow. Untested behavior and application security sit beyond that conclusion.

A passing workflow is evidence for that scenario. It does not validate all AWS behavior or application security.

Diagram shows AWS's pass rule, not a particular test result or measured coverage. Application security still requires testing on real AWS before production.

Qualitative diagram of AWS's published fidelity definition and testing limits. Branches compare the real-AWS reference with emulator replay; they do not represent simultaneous live tests, amounts or coverage proportions.

Diagram shows AWS's pass rule, not a particular test result or measured coverage. Application security still requires testing on real AWS before production.

Security has a separate limit. AWS's security guidance warns against using the emulator to determine whether an application is secure. It does not check AWS KMS key policies or Amazon S3 bucket policies, and a request denied by AWS may succeed locally.

Agent review of implementation security therefore cannot be read as validation of a user's application permissions. The emulator is for building and testing, not production workloads. AWS instructs developers to test their whole application and security settings on real AWS before production.

For builders adopting agent-written software, the release makes the acceptance process as relevant as the code's authorship: which behaviors are checked, what remains outside coverage, and where the developer must still test against the real service.

When it comes to pubic hair trimming, it’s all about balancing risk versus results. When you’re trimming or shaving delicate skin below the belt, you need to be careful, and this trimmer helps minimize risk. Specifically designed for your groin area, the blades are more closely spaced to help prevent snags, and the attachments help protect your skin from direct contact with the razor.

Testing Notes: This trimmer makes the case for using tools specifically designed for the area you’re grooming. I found in my testing that its blades are more closely placed than your traditional trimmer to help prevent skin from being caught between them. They actually make a difference when trimming your delicate nether regions.

All the features packed into this trimmer make the experience of trimming your groin as easy as possible and minimize cut risk, while the skin-protecting attachment does a great job of providing further distance between your skin and the blade. The one thing to note about this trimmer, however, is that if you prefer a clean shave, this will not deliver it by itself.

While it will trim very close, even with the attachment, it’s not going to give you a smooth, clean finish. You may want to use this trimmer to trim down the carpet first before moving in with a traditional razor. Also, if you’re hoping to trim other parts of your body, like your head or face (which I wouldn’t recommend for sanitary reasons), you may not find this trimmer powerful enough for the thicker hair that’s found in those locations.

Honestly, is there something the Philips OneBlade can’t do? Since its launch, this trimmer and shaver has become an iconic grooming essential, and for good reason. It’s incredibly easy to use, hardly ever nicks or cuts skin, and can shave and trim with equally good results. This version even comes with more length attachments that allow you to get your ideal manscaping results with ease.

Testing Notes: In all of my trimmer and shaver testing, no matter what kind, the Philips OneBlade stands out among the pack because it’s just so darn easy to use. Unlike your typical trimmers, the innovative head is shaped like a razor and can cut hair in both directions, making it foolproof.

There is also something about the razor, even when used without any attachments, that hardly ever cuts skin, even when you’re using it on your delicate areas below the belt. Since it’s designed for body grooming, the OneBlade features more attachments than the original, but you still won’t be able to leave hair super long.

The plus side of getting quite as close as other trimming options means it’s nearly impossible to cut yourself—even if you’re using it without a guard. Whenever someone is nervous about nicking their nuts, this is my top recommendation.

It’s best for people who like a close trim or a shave. The small size and light weight make it easy to take with you wherever you go, and I had no issue with the battery life, even though it’s not quite as long as some others on this list.

I also appreciate that it comes with a second blade, so you can easily switch them when you use this on your face (you don’t want to use the same blade on your face and body because of the possibility of cross-contamination).

Read more: Philips Norelco OneBlade Review

This trimmer is chock-full of cool features that are the sort of thing you didn’t know you needed until you have them, like a built-in LED light for seamless groinal navigation, a travel lock to avoid slicing through clothes or other products in your Dopp kit, and a nifty low-battery light to let you know it’s time to recharge before diving into a trim.

This trimmer is built for below-the-belt grooming but works great on other body parts too. It trims quickly and efficiently, no matter where you use it. The 5.0 is also fully waterproof and armed with a protective outer guard above the blades to minimize the risk of nicks or cuts.

Testing Notes: In my testing, I found a lot to love about the newest version of the Lawn Mower. Compared to previous models, it seems to cut a little bit easier and more efficiently, and with less snagging. The blade guard really does help in this department, though I did experience a few nicks when trying to trim too quickly (never a good idea when dealing with the groin, to be honest).

I don’t recommend using it without the guard, as the blades can be a little harsh on bare skin. However, a natural side effect of this is that you won’t ever get a completely bald shave with this device. Still, it’s surprisingly lightweight, and the added features like the built-in light make the experience of groin trimming as pleasant as it can be. It also corrected one of the more annoying issues with previous models by adding a travel lock on its power button that requires more effort to activate.

Unlike previous models, the 5.0 does not include a charging dock; however, it is fully equipped with USB-C charging capabilities, which I much prefer to the dock. I’d argue that every electric device should be required to use this much more universal charger. It saves on space by limiting the amount of wires you need laying around, and is far more convenient to replace if you ever lose the included cord.

Read More: Manscaped Chairman Plus Review

Meridian’s body trimmer helps prevent irritation, tugging, and nicks with its high-precision ceramic blades. Slicing your skin when manscaping, especially if you’re new to it, can produce serious panic, which is why Meridian went with ceramic blades. In comparison to steel or plastic, ceramic blades stay sharper longer, generate less heat, and glide smoothly across sensitive skin.

This makes Meridian’s trimmer ideal for beginners or anyone nervous about trimming sensitive areas. Plus, it’s waterproof and easy to use. There aren’t any complicated settings or tech involved, and just two guards to choose from. For beginners, this is perfect. It limits any learning curve beyond getting over the initial hump of anxiety for where you’re taking a blade.

Testing Notes: Meridian highlights two key benefits of its pubic trimmer: safety and speed—even claiming you can finish a full job in under 60 seconds. While I can confirm it’s powerful enough to mow through hair fast, no one should approach grooming with that expectation. Rushing, especially on sensitive areas, is a quick way to end up with nicks and cuts.

In terms of safety, I found this trimmer rarely—if ever—caused cuts or irritation. However, that safety seems to come at the cost of precision. I often had to go over the same spot multiple times to get a close shave. While the ceramic blades boost protection, they just don’t shave as closely as stainless steel.

Braun built this trimmer to power through all kinds of hair, no matter the length or location. With adjustable settings offering up to 40 lengths, it trims nose hairs just as easily as it delivers a crew cut. Its powerful motor and precision make it a top choice for anyone with thick body hair or an untamed look down below, where other trimmers often fall short.

Testing Notes: I love the wide-ranging length options the Braun All-In-One Series 9 offers that allow for true head-to-toe grooming. The adjustable length dial particularly makes transitioning from one part of your body to another seamless and quick for those in a hurry. Now, I wouldn’t recommend using the same trimmer for your face and body, but this device certainly has the agility and horsepower to handle all areas smoothly.

I also dig how sleek the charging dock is and, crucially, how little space it takes up on the bathroom counter. That being said, while Braun boasts about the Series 9’s 180-minute charging runtime, my testing found it’s in the 120-minute range. Still an impressive burst from one charge, but not quite 180 minutes.

Read More: Braun Series 9 Style Kit Review

Using a disposable razor for pubic shaving is great because it minimizes the risk of cross-contamination, and you ensure that your blades are always sharp and ready to cut. This disposable razor has five gentle blades that, while not specifically designed for the groin, are designed for the most sensitive skin, making it perfect for the area.

Testing Notes: Conventional wisdom says that using fewer blades is ideal for shaving the pubic area, as razors with multiple blades often increase the risk of irritation, razor bumps, and ingrown hairs. These issues tend to arise when the blades cut hair beneath the skin’s surface, creating friction and complicating regrowth.

In contrast, a single- or double-blade razor trims hair cleanly at the surface, reducing skin damage and delivering a smoother, gentler shave. But I found the BIC Flex 5 Sensitive razor to be the best of both worlds. Covering the ground of a five-blade razor with the softness of a one-blade razor.

Not only did it speed up the admittedly long process of pubic shaving, but it did so without destroying my most delicate skin. The only trade-off here is that this razor doesn’t get quite as close as other, less-gentle blades. Still, it gets much closer than the trimmers on this list, and nearly as close as the Gillette Intimate Razor. Besides, going entirely bald down here is rarely a goal of mine, so I saw this as a positive.

If you’re looking to go as close to bald as possible, this is your best option. Designed specifically for body grooming, this razor features a compact, ultra-grippy handle that minimizes the risk of dropping and helps you maintain control while in the shower (or contorting yourself to reach every part of your groin). The blades are about as spaced out from each other as I’ve seen on any razor, which helps prevent clogging—something that is even more common when dealing with thick body hair.

Surrounding the two blades are a lubricating strip, an anti-ingrown bar, and an anti-irritation bar that work to reduce friction and help prevent trapped hairs. Plus, the blade head sits on a flexible pivoting disc, which helps the razor follow the contours of your body for smoother, more consistent contact with the skin.

Testing Notes: I’m not usually one to go completely bald below the waist, but this razor makes a strong case for it. It left my skin smooth and irritation-free without any lingering bumps in the days following, which is something I’ve found to be common when dealing with body razors. The grip is incredible and the pivoting head makes getting into the nooks and crannies of your body easy.

Before diving into the most intimate of manscaping, it’s important to consider a few key components of the device you’ll be using, given the sensitivity of the region. Not only to avoid any dreaded nicks or cuts, but also to ensure that the process is completed as seamlessly as possible.

Whenever you’re dealing with a trimmer of any kind, the battery life is one of the most prominent considerations. No one wants their device to sputter out and die when they’ve only managed to trim half their beard, and the same is true for the nether regions. Sure, it may be less noticeable than having half a beard, but it can still be uncomfortable. Look for devices that can hold a charge for at least an hour; this should guarantee you two to three sessions per charge.

Any less and you’re going to have to really be diligent with charging after every use or run the risk of it dying out before the next job’s done. The easiest way to avoid this scenario is to look for a rechargeable device, but more on that in a sec.

If you’re a committed pubic trimmer and never travel without one, look for the lighter options to ensure you can comfortably keep them in a carry-on or bag without weighing yourself down. While the TSA and airlines do not generally have a weight limit specifically for grooming devices, they do limit the weight of your bags, so we recommend sticking to trimmers that are under 10 oz to avoid too much bulk. Plus, if you’re new to this type of thing, steering away from tools that are heavier than this until you get a better idea of the process will help you avoid any painful slip-ups.

Similarly, how often do you change up your overall manscaping look? If you find yourself often changing up lengths and styles, you’re going to want to grab a device with multiple attachments and length options. The Braun Series 9 is the best-case scenario here, as it comes packed with nine attachments that create a total of 40 (!) length options. On the other hand, if you typically go full bald or keep it one consistent length, focus on the device’s head shape and blade material or close shaving ability rather than the number of attachments.

For the closest shave (outside of a cartridge razor), look to stainless steel or metal blades, as these can handle the most motor power and are more adept at plowing through thicker hair. While most of the trimmers on this list (and pubic trimmers in general) do not list their official motor power, having stainless steel blades is often the best indicator of a powerful tool, as it shows the brand looks towards the highest quality materials and performance available.

Not to mention, stainless steel blades are typically easier to clean. That being said, the risk of nicks and cuts is higher, so if you’re new to pubic trimming, opt for ceramic or plastic blades. These are gentler on skin, though they won’t get you as close to bare skin.

Use a rechargeable pubic trimmer to avoid mid-trim shutdowns and eliminate the need for spare batteries. Keep it charged between 30 percent and 80 percent to maintain performance and prevent it from dying when you need it most.

Do you prefer to do your manscaping in or outside of the shower? There is no wrong answer, but whichever you prefer is worth keeping in mind when choosing a trimmer. Some are made to be used wet, like the Philips Norelco OneBlade, while others not so much. If you’re a dedicated shower groomer, focus on the fully waterproof options.

As Men’s Health’s grooming editor, I test electric razors and similar devices for a living. When it comes to pubic trimmers, we’ve been testing these devices for nearly three years since this story was first published in 2023. For this update, I tested or retested over 15 pubic trimmers and razors, while consulting with skin and haircare experts on which tools they recommend in 2026.

I also considered top-reviewed trimmers that had high customer ratings on trusted e-commerce websites. After putting each device to the test, I evaluated its effectiveness, safety, and value. Following 12 months of testing, these seven tools proved to be the best for the job.

1. First and foremost, make sure you have ample time and are not rushed. This is not something you want to speed through.

2. Position yourself in front of a mirror with good lighting to make sure you have good visibility for all the crevices.

3. Grab your trimmer and pick your desired length. If you plan to fully shave your pubic hair, set the length long enough to shave easily but not too long—about a couple of days’ worth of stubble. If you’re trimming, start with a longer setting than you want at first; you can always trim it shorter later.

4. Apply baby powder on your pubic area while it’s dry to help soak up extra moisture and plump up the hair.

5. With short, gentle strokes, use the trimmer to cut the hair. Pubic hair grows in a variety of directions, so you’ll want to go slow and possibly go over the same areas a few times. For your scrotum and shaft, go extra slow and stretch the skin to flatten it and make it easier to trim. If you’re trimming your buttcheeks, crack, or perineum, you may want to place a hand mirror on the floor to help see where you’re trimming. You can also place one leg on a tub or toilet to make the area easier to see.

6. If you’re happy with the trim job, then you’re done! Hop in the shower to wash off.

7. If you’re going to shave completely, once you’re out of the shower, apply a pre-shave oil and shaving cream to the areas you’re going to shave. The key here is not to be stingy with the cream.

8. When you’re taking a razor to your nether regions, you’ll want to be extra careful. Shave with the grain of the hair in short, slow strokes. Do not—I repeat—do not rush. You’ll want to use the same stretching technique on your scrotum and shaft as you did while trimming, and the mirror is ideal if you’re taking the razor around back.

9. Make sure to rinse the razor frequently to avoid clogs and reapply shaving cream as needed.

10. Once you’re done, hop back in the shower to rinse everything away.

11. Apply a moisturizer or body oil to the area to help keep it protected. You may also want to apply a moisturizer or anti-chafe product regularly (like at least once a day) to help reduce friction, which can cause irritation on shaved skin, especially below the belt.

Maybe you’re a regular manscaper, or perhaps you just took the plunge into trimming out your nether regions. Regardless, one truth holds true: As soon as you take off the hair, it blooms right back again.

Sure, it might seem that your pubic hair is on a steroid-fueled regrowth. But that’s actually something of an optic illusion, says Dr. Alexes Hazen, MD, a reconstructive and cosmetic plastic surgeon at NYU Langone Health.

People who trim or shave their pubic hair often believe it grows faster than the hair on their head, but that’s a misconception, she says. We merely notice hair growth more and its speed when it’s shorter.

With pubic hair—and other body hair—the entire process takes about 30 to 44 days, Dr. Hazen says. That means the same pubes that started to grow will shed in about a month to a month and a half.

#5154. Bitcoin Price Briefly Crashes to $67,500, Lowest Since August, as Dollar Holds 19-Month High

Bitcoin price traded near $69,800 on Friday morning after briefly crashing to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern, its lowest level since mid-August, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The rebound held after October producer prices rose less than economists had expected, though the U.S. dollar remained near a 19-month high and traders still fully priced a December Federal Reserve rate hike.

Bitcoin price was trading near $72,800 at this time Thursday. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then gave way late at night, breaking below $70,000 and sliding to that midnight low. The move also pushed the bitcoin price below its 200-week moving average, a long-term trend line near $68,000. Buyers lifted it back above $69,000 before sunrise, and the rebound extended toward $69,800 after the producer-price report.

The U.S. Dollar Index held above 103 Friday after a three-day rally took it to its highest level since April 2025. The 10-year Treasury yield was near 5.15% ahead of the data, and two-year yields, which track Fed expectations most closely, were on pace for their worst week since 2024, Bloomberg reported.

Traders still see an 88% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting and a 12% chance of a half-point move, CME FedWatch data show. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has added a 50-basis-point increase to the discussion, and New York Fed President John Williams said Thursday that inflation remains high and policymakers need to take further action.

Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar tends to drain demand for risk assets. Both have pressured the bitcoin price since this week’s hotter-than-expected consumer price index.

Bitcoin has also broken from tech stocks. It fell 5.9% between Nov. 5 and Nov. 12 while the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.4%, a sign it is trading more on yields and the dollar than on the AI trade. Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 0.6% Friday after the producer-price report, as investors also weighed Nvidia’s announcement that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO.

The break below $70,000 set off a wave of forced selling. About $1.64 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with bets on higher prices making up nearly 89% of the total and bitcoin positions accounting for $916 million.

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs added to the pressure. The funds posted about $47.7 million in net outflows Thursday, their sixth straight day of withdrawals, bringing the run to roughly $1.49 billion. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) alone bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday, and the group has now flipped to about $1.56 billion in net outflows for 2026.

Sentiment has soured with it. A widely watched crypto fear and greed gauge dropped to 20 Friday, its lowest reading since July 8, and bitcoin is now on track for a second straight down year.

Positioning has turned defensive. Average perpetual futures funding rates turned negative for the first time in a month as the price fell toward $68,500, meaning short sellers are now paying to hold their bets. Order books are also thin. Bitcoin order-book depth across major exchanges fell to $72 million on Nov. 9, roughly 33% below normal levels. “Liquidity remains thin while leverage stays elevated, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp moves in either direction,” said Tanay Ved, a senior research associate at Talos.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% monthly increase economists had expected, after a revised 1.4% advance in September. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, increased 0.3%, matching forecasts. On an unadjusted basis, the headline index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler report took some pressure off the dollar, which still held above 103, but a December rate hike remains fully priced, leaving limited relief for the bitcoin price heading into the weekend.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $69,800.

#5152. Aave plan could cut some lenders’ share of interest by 60%

Polygon DAI lenders would keep just 30% of borrower interest under the proposal, down from 75%, as Aave’s treasury takes a larger share.

Aave lenders supplying DAI on Polygon could see their share of borrower interest fall from 75% to 30% under a November 12 proposal by TokenLogic. The plan would redirect more interest to Aave’s DAO treasury, with uneven cuts to lender returns across its markets.

The November 12 proposal covers 54 reserves across 12 Aave V3 instances and Ethereum V2. TokenLogic estimates about $4 million in additional annualized DAO revenue using November 9 balances and rates. That total includes roughly $1 million from Plasma USDT0, a change that would enter the formal proposal only once its terms are finalized.

In Aave’s lending system, the mechanism is the reserve factor: the portion of borrower interest allocated to the DAO instead of suppliers. Raising it changes who receives the interest, without directly changing the borrowing-rate curve. TokenLogic argues the larger share would better compensate the DAO for the risks attached to borrowable reserves.

Polygon V3 DAI illustrates how much that allocation can matter. TokenLogic proposes raising its reserve factor from 25% to 70%, with a modeled supply APY reduction of 270 basis points, or 2.70 percentage points. The same line projects $94,373 in additional annual DAO revenue.

With the amount of borrower interest unchanged, suppliers’ share would fall from 75% to 30%. The treasury would receive the difference. In that fixed-input model, the revenue gain comes from a smaller payment to lenders, without requiring more borrowing or a higher price for the same loan.

Polygon DAI illustrates TokenLogic’s November 12 proposal: the interest allocation changes while the model holds borrowing and rates fixed.

The proposed 70% reserve factor leaves suppliers 30% of borrower interest, down from 75%.

Proposal-listed current and proposed factors, not execution evidence. Total borrower interest is held fixed; subsequent liquidity or rate responses can change realized income. The shares concern lending interest, not deposit principal.

Supplier share = 100% minus reserve factor: 100-25=75 and 100-70=30. DAO share rises by 70-25=45 percentage points. Verified with JavaScript arithmetic; bar widths scale linearly to a fixed 600-unit desktop or 312-unit mobile interest pool. This is derived allocation arithmetic, not an APY calculation.

Proposal-listed current and proposed factors, not execution evidence. Total borrower interest is held fixed; subsequent liquidity or rate responses can change realized income. The shares concern lending interest, not deposit principal.

The comparison with other stablecoins shows that the proposal does not apply a uniform yield reduction. TokenLogic models cuts of 173 basis points for Avalanche DAI.e, 78 for Avalanche USDt and 61 for Avalanche USDC. Their proposed reserve factors are 90%, 25% and 25%, respectively.

For savers choosing where to lend stablecoins, those reductions change the return offered for keeping liquidity in the affected reserve. TokenLogic identifies Polygon DAI as a legacy reserve and explicitly uses lower returns as an incentive to move liquidity out of declining markets.

Modeled supply APY changes in TokenLogic’s November 12 proposal using November 9, 2026 balances and rates. Negative values are reductions; 100 basis points equals 1 percentage point. Selected reserves, not the complete proposal.

Source: TokenLogic proposal; model inputs November 9, 2026

A separate Aavescan observation puts the Polygon DAI pool in perspective. Its November 12 midnight-UTC snapshot records 3.30 million DAI deposited, 2.65 million borrowed and a 4.81% supply APR, excluding historical incentives.

Aavescan’s observed APR and TokenLogic’s modeled APY reduction, based on November 9 inputs, describe different rate measures at different dates.

The largest reserve-factor percentages do not necessarily impose the largest yield cuts. TokenLogic proposes 100% factors for selected bitcoin-wrapper and liquid-staking collateral reserves whose lending APYs are already close to zero. Its model puts the lost lending yield in that group at no more than 1 to 2 basis points.

A 100% reserve factor applies to lending interest, not deposit principal. For wstETH, it is also separate from the staking accrual reflected in the token’s stETH value. Redirecting Aave’s incremental lending interest would leave that underlying accrual mechanism intact.

Plasma USDT0 shows why a modest yield cut can still produce a large revenue estimate. TokenLogic models a reserve-factor increase from 5% to 7.5% against about $632 million borrowed. The projected supply APY reduction is 16 basis points, alongside about $1 million in additional annual revenue. Its inclusion remains conditional on finalized Plasma terms.

Even for the other lines, annualizing November 9 balances and rates holds the inputs fixed. The proposal also seeks to change supplier behavior, which could alter those inputs.

For Ethereum V2, TokenLogic proposes raising five remaining borrowed reserves to 99.99%, directing nearly all their interest to the DAO. It expects reduced returns to encourage exits. If suppliers withdraw, utilization could rise and borrowing costs could increase, creating pressure on borrowers to close positions.

Aave’s utilization-based borrowing curve links borrowing costs to how much liquidity is in use. That potential response is separate from changing the curve itself, as in the USDT borrowing-rule update CryptoSlate covered in October.

The November 12 publication lists feedback and escalation to the Aave Improvement Proposal stage as next steps. Its yield cuts and revenue gains remain proposed estimates.

Whether it's a hot day or you're working up a sweat at the gym, Airism pulls moisture away from your skin, making sure you don't feel swampy down under.

Every Sunday at my house is wash day, but this underwear has survived through every last cycle without losing its allure. Our only gripe is that Uniqlo Airism sells out very fast, which means you have to wait for the occasional restock—so get them now.

Cotton is the OG of underwear fabrics, and our testers found that it's the most comfortable knit for everyday fits. Take note: while cotton is pretty breathable, it doesn't do a great job of wicking away moisture. That's why our fashion editors do not recommend cotton skivvies for working out. In some cases, a pair of undies that's 100% cotton tends to lose shape over time and can give a swamp-ass feeling. If you have money to spend, we recommend trying a long-staple or organic cotton, which is more premium and durable.

Nylon is moisture-wicking and super durable, so the fabric won’t pill or stretch out. However, a little spandex (aka elastane) in the fabric helps for movement and extra comfort. Plus, it dries quickly too, so you won't feel sticky post-workout.

Imagine cotton, but smoother and a little fancier. Modal has a silky-soft feel that's light and cool against your skin. Testers say their favorite modal boxer briefs almost disappear under their clothes.

If you're looking to keep your precious cargo secure, then briefs provide the most security. However, if you want to let the package breathe, then boxers are your best bet. Remember: Boxers tend to ride up when you're wearing slim pants, which is why we recommend only wearing them with more relaxed fits.

If you need extra support, we recommend underwear with a pouch or a snugger fit around the waistband. For some men with testicular pain or discomfort, they may want to find a style that fits well and doesn't ride up or bunch, as this could aggravate their symptoms.

Your underwear is the first thing you put on and the last thing you take off, so it has to work with you, not against you, all day long. If it doesn't do its job, you'll feel it, whether it's discomfort, chafing, or overheating.

Think about it: excellent underwear isn't just about looking cool (though that's like icing on the cake). It's about how it performs in real life. Are you lounging at home? Going for a long run? Stuck on a flight for hours? Each of these scenarios demands something different. You need underwear that supports your lifestyle, whether that's stretch for flexibility, moisture-wicking for sweat, or breathability to keep things fresh down yonder.

The best breathable underwear manages heat and moisture so sweat can escape instead of getting trapped against your skin. Many use micro-knit or mesh-like weaves that create tiny air channels within the fabric, allowing heat to dissipate and air to circulate as you move. Others incorporate moisture-wicking fibers to pull sweat away from the body and spread it across the surface of the fabric so it evaporates faster. Some brands even add targeted “cool zones” or thinner panels in high-sweat areas to boost airflow where you need it most.

When underwear can’t breathe, moisture builds up, leading to overheating, chafing, irritation, and odor. Breathable underwear works with your body by keeping things cooler, drier, and more comfortable throughout the day. For Men’s Health guys, breathability makes a difference for everyday wear, long commutes, desk jobs, workouts, travel days, and humid conditions. It’s especially clutch for guys who sweat easily, live in hot climates, train hard, or spend long stretches in the same pair from morning to night.

As part of the Men’s Health style team, led by our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, I’ve tested some of the best—and worst—underwear on the market firsthand. Since 2015, our team has worn, washed, and stressed-tested more than 100 pairs across every major style, brand, and fabric imaginable, from classic cotton briefs to high-tech performance boxer briefs and luxe everyday upgrades.

Testing wasn't limited to just one body type or fit preference. In addition to my own wear tests, multiple Men's Health editors with different builds pitched in, spanning sizes from small through XXL. This allowed us to see how each pair fit and performed across a wide range of body types, rises, thigh sizes, and proportions—and to flag issues like inconsistent sizing, rolling waistbands, or fabric that only works on one kind of frame.

I wore each pair repeatedly in real-life situations, including workdays, workouts, commutes, travel, and weekend outings. I looked at how each pair performed over time, paying close attention to whether fabrics remained soft without pilling, waistbands held their shape, seams avoided chafing, and support held up after hours of movement. I judged each pair on fabric quality, fit, breathability, odor control, stretch and recovery, durability after repeated washes, and comfort levels ranging from morning to night. Only the pairs that consistently delivered comfort, support, and long-term performance earned a spot on this list. What you’ll find here are the top 12 best men’s underwear options that rose to the top after years of hands-on testing by the Men’s Health team.

Boxers: They’re classic, loose-fitting shorts that are lightweight, with lots of breathing room, and zero restriction. They’re great for lounging or sleeping because they feel airy and relaxed, but that same looseness makes them less practical under slim pants. Fabric can bunch, ride up, and offer little to no support if you’re moving around a lot. Boxer briefs: They’re cut like boxers but fit snugly like briefs. That means they hug your thighs, hold everything in place, and layer smoothly under jeans, trousers, or even gym shorts. They also prevent chafing since the fabric creates a barrier between your thighs—a lifesaver if you walk a lot or hit the gym. The tradeoff? They’re less airy than boxers, but most guys prefer the balance of comfort, coverage, and support.

That really depends on your laundry schedule. If you’re someone who does laundry once a week, aim for at least 10 to 12 pairs so you’ve got a little cushion. If laundry happens less often—say every two weeks—you’ll probably want 15 to 20 pairs. If you’re very active, then consider stocking your drawer with 25 to 30 pairs. Basically, you want enough to last until wash day plus a couple extra for workouts, surprise trips, or the occasional lazy Sunday when you just don’t feel like doing laundry.

A good rule of thumb: it’s reasonable to refresh your stash every six to 12 months, but quality underwear can last longer depending on fabric, frequency of wear, washing, and condition. If the elastic’s shot, they’re sagging, developing holes, or the fabric’s thinning, that’s your cue to toss them. Think of it as a rotation—you don’t need to replace everything at once, but gradually swap in new pairs so you’re always stocked with comfortable, supportive ones.

Every man has worn them at some point; boxers are light and loose and so freeing. They're the classic underwear style for men that feels very relaxed with short legs. This type of underwear is perfect for lounging around the house, sleeping, or wearing under relaxed-fit pants. Also comes in a variety of prints and patterns (hello, personality).

Think speedo. Think upside-down triangle. Briefs provide the required coverage and optimal support while exposing more skin for ease of mobility. Here, there's no risk of leg fabric riding up (because there's none).

Perhaps the most popular one, it's a hybrid of loose-fit boxers and tight briefs, offering a solid balance of support and comfort. If you’re not a fan of underwear that rides up too high, go for boxer briefs that have a longer leg and a snug fit, like compression underwear that’s perfect for the gym. They should skim the leg versus squeezing you too tight.

Like the title says, a trunk is similar to boxer briefs but with a shorter cut—halfway up the thigh. It's best for guys who want something fitted but less fabric around the leg. For some visual assistance, think of trunks as the underwear style that most CK models wear on big billboards.

It depends on personal preference, comfort, and the activity. Here's a quick breakdown to help guide your choice, weighing the pros and cons of both.

Tight underwear (e.g., briefs, boxer briefs) provides better support, which is especially useful for physical activities like running or working out. This type reduces chafing and prevents excessive movement, which can help with comfort throughout the day. Works well under slim-fit pants, as it avoids bunching and creates a cleaner silhouette. If it's too tight, it can restrict airflow and potentially cause discomfort or sweating, especially in warmer weather. Overly tight fits might not be ideal for guys concerned about reproductive health, though the effect is typically negligible with properly sized underwear.

On the other hand, loose underwear is better suited for lounging or casual, low-impact activities since it allows more airflow and freedom of movement. It feels more breathable, making it ideal for hotter climates or relaxed settings. Also, loose underwear can be paired with loose-fit pants for added comfort. This option lacks support, which feel uncomfortable during workouts or physical activity. Plus, it can cramp your style—bunching up under tighter pants and offering a restrictive feel.

If you want to protect the structural integrity of your underwear's waistband, the best way to keep them from stretching is to hand wash them and hang them dry. But given how impractical that is, the second best option is to put them in the washing machine on cold water and use a low dryer setting so the elastic doesn't warp. However, our testers say that most of the pairs they've tried have kept their waistbands' shapes even after several trips to the laundromat. If your underwear's waistband has lost its shape, you're probably overdue to replace it.

Even the best underwear won’t last if you don’t take care of it properly. Washing underwear inside out helps remove sweat and bacteria more effectively while protecting the fabric’s surface. Cold or warm water is usually best, as hot water can break down elastic fibers and cause shrinkage over time. Skip harsh detergents and fabric softeners, especially for performance or moisture-wicking underwear. Softeners can coat fibers and reduce breathability and odor control. When possible, air-drying is ideal, as high heat from dryers is the fastest way to kill stretch and warp waistbands. If you do use a dryer, stick to low heat.

#5147. President Trump Taps Two Democrats in Bipartisan Slate of SEC and CFTC Nominees as Both Agencies Run Short-Handed

President Donald Trump sent the Senate four nominees for the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission on Thursday, his first picks for either agency in about a year and the first Democrats he has put forward for them.

Former CFTC Commissioner Kristin Johnson, a Democrat, and Republican Steven Levine were nominated to the SEC. Republican Nathan Anonick and Democrat Matthew Rowland were nominated to the CFTC, Bloomberg Law reported.

Each nominee needs Senate confirmation. The Senate Banking Committee will handle the SEC picks, while the Senate Agriculture Committee will take up the CFTC pair before any vote by the full chamber.

Levine was tapped for the SEC seat left by Hester Peirce, whose term expired, for a term running through June 5, 2030. He most recently served as general counsel and a senior adviser at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and previously worked at the SEC as counsel and deputy chief of staff to Commissioner Mark Uyeda.

Peirce led the SEC’s Crypto Task Force and was one of the agency’s most vocal supporters of clearer crypto rules.

Johnson would take the seat formerly held by Democrat Caroline Crenshaw, for a term ending June 5, 2029. She served as a CFTC commissioner until 2025 and is a former law school professor. During her time at the CFTC, she spoke often about digital assets, including custody and decentralized finance.

Both CFTC nominees come from the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the derivatives regulator. Anonick is legislative counsel to Chairman John Boozman and was a lead negotiator on the committee’s portion of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031.

Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee who also worked on the Clarity Act and the committee’s 2024 crypto bill. He previously served on Johnson’s staff at the CFTC, according to his LinkedIn profile. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028.

Both agencies can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from one party. The SEC currently has two, Chairman Paul Atkins and Commissioner Mark Uyeda. Chairman Mike Selig is the CFTC’s only sitting commissioner.

The timing puts the nominees in front of a Senate in its lame-duck session, weeks after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s sharpest critics, is expected to chair the Banking Committee when the new Congress is seated in January.

The pairing of Democrats with Republicans could matter for confirmation. After the election, TD Cowen’s Jaret Seiberg told clients he did not expect Democrats to confirm Trump nominees unless the president filled Democratic seats at agencies such as the SEC, a step he called unlikely. Thursday’s slate does exactly that at both regulators.

The nominations also land with crypto market structure legislation stalled. The Clarity Act failed a Senate cloture vote 49-50 on Sept. 15 and dies on Jan. 3 unless the lame-duck session revives it.

Without new law, the SEC and CFTC have set crypto policy largely on their own this year. Selig’s CFTC opened the door to equity perpetual futures, and a federal judge later said the agency likely overstepped while letting trading continue.

The White House did not say when it expects the Senate to act. The open question is whether a Senate heading for Democratic control moves the four nominees before January, or leaves the SEC and CFTC running with skeleton commissions into 2027.
