Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Inside the shoes and layers the endurance athlete relies on for steep climbs.

RÉMI BONNET MAKES running up mountains look easy. The Swiss endurance athlete holds the world record for the vertical kilometer, having climbed more than 3,200 feet in just 27 minutes and 21 seconds. It’s the equivalent of running nearly three Empire State Buildings straight up in less than half an hour.

That's why Tudor, Rolex's adventurous younger brother and one of our favorite watch brands, tapped the 31-year-old athlete for its “Born to Dare” campaign, which celebrates high-achieving risk-takers. For Bonnet, that partnership means "daring to take risks, daring to try new things, and daring to push the limit a bit further."

When Men's Health caught up with Bonnet in Chamonix, France, during UTMB Mont-Blanc, one of the world's most prestigious trail-running events, he shared how his gear has evolved over the years. While he once obsessed over shaving every possible gram off his equipment, he's learned that lighter isn't always better, especially when it comes to performance.

We asked Bonnet to share the six pieces of gear he swears by, from his favorite trail-running shoes to a blister-prevention product.

As a Tudor ambassador, Bonnet has his pick of some seriously handsome watches, but the Ranger is his favorite. We're also big fans. Inspired by Tudor’s history of exploration, this rugged field watch features a stainless steel case, scratch-resistant sapphire crystal, and water resistance up to 100 meters, so it can take a licking. With multiple case sizes and strap options (stainless steel bracelet! Fabric strap! Rubber!), you can find one that fits your vibe, whether you're dressing up for dinner or heading outdoors.

Bonnet relies on Normatec compression boots after grueling races and long flights. The latest Elite model is completely wireless, with up to four hours of battery life, making it easy to squeeze in a leg massage whether you're at home or on the road. It also offers seven pressure settings to customize the intensity. A Men’s Health tester found the boots helped relieve his tired legs after a tough workout, and he even fell asleep during a 60-minute session.

Read more: Hyperice Normatec Elite Review

Before races, Bonnet puts on this anti-chafing cream. A blend of shea butter forms a thin, sweat-resistant barrier to help prevent blisters and friction mile after mile.

Bonnet loves these trail-running socks, which feature targeted cushioning in high-pressure areas like the heels and balls of the feet, plus moisture-wicking fabric to keep his feet dry mile after mile. They're also designed with extra support around the ankles to help lock the socks in place on uneven terrain.

As a Salomon-sponsored athlete, Bonnet is already running in the upcoming S/Lab Pulsar 5. "It is a mix between lightness and the performance of a road shoe," he says. Until that model hits shelves, the Pulsar 4 is the next best thing. It weighs just 9 ounces and features a dual-foam midsole, abrasion-resistant Matryx upper, and 3.5-millimeter rubber lugs for traction on rocky trails.

Bonnet uses an Insta360 camera to document his mountain adventures for Instagram. We're also fans of the brand, having awarded its GO Ultra a Men’s Health Tech Award in 2026. The latest X6 shoots sharp 8K video, with impressive image stabilization that keeps footage smooth even when you're shredding down a mountain. Its invisible selfie stick disappears from your footage for drone-like shots without needing someone else to film you.

#5144. FBI warns active $400M crypto scam targets your friends by replacing your face in videos

The FBI says North Korean hackers reuse stolen accounts and webcam footage to draw the next contact into a fake meeting.

North Korean hackers are using stolen webcam recordings to impersonate crypto workers in fake meetings with their contacts, turning one victim's familiar face into bait for the next attack, the FBI warns.

The Justice Department announced disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used in FaceStealer on November 12. It said the scheme had caused more than $400 million in cryptocurrency theft over the preceding 18 months and that the FBI had seized over 900 victim webcam videos under a federal warrant.

The DOJ release treats FaceStealer separately from the Binance theft, which CryptoSlate has covered through the FBI's attribution and the exchange's asset-replenishment delays.

In its November 12 FLASH advisory, the FBI describes attackers taking over genuine accounts on services including Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord. Access to chat histories lets them tailor an invitation to earlier conversations, giving a new approach the context of an existing relationship.

A legitimate calendaring service can handle the scheduling. The malicious meeting link arrives shortly before the call, directing the target to a copycat Zoom or Microsoft Teams session controlled by the attackers.

Once the target enters, stored webcam footage makes it appear that the known contact has joined. Attackers can simulate several participants. The familiar person on screen can therefore be a real prior victim's recording, rather than a live participant.

The FBI says FaceStealer still overwhelmingly relies on stolen genuine videos. Generated deepfakes provide an additional way to impersonate participants.

The target's webcam becomes part of the attack before the supposed troubleshooting begins. The FLASH says recording starts when the target first clicks the imposter meeting link. The attackers can later use that footage to impersonate the target.

That is where the scheme joins theft to impersonation. Access to the computer can expose cryptocurrency or other valuable access. Stolen communication accounts, contact lists and webcam footage give the hackers material for the next approach. The FBI's FaceStealer resource page describes the same cycle of compromise, account hijacking and fake meetings.

The damage is not necessarily immediate. The FBI reported cases in which cryptocurrency theft and communication-account takeovers came months to more than a year after the initial compromise. A quiet period after a suspicious meeting therefore does not establish that a device or account is safe.

A condensed view of the attack sequence described in the FBI's November 12 advisory.

Opening the imposter meeting link records webcam footage; following the fake fix installs malware.

The cycle shows reuse, not a fixed timetable or every encounter. The FBI says genuine stolen footage predominates, while generated deepfakes are also used.

Editorial condensation of the FBI's reported attack cycle. Arrows show reuse of compromised accounts and footage, not a fixed timetable, growth rate or new calculation.

The cycle shows reuse, not a fixed timetable or every encounter. The FBI says genuine stolen footage predominates, while generated deepfakes are also used.

The FBI recommends using the official meeting application with an invite code and, where possible, confirming an invitation through a different communication channel. That checks the approach beyond the account the attacker may already control.

It also advises delaying webcam activation until the inviter can be seen, heard and communicated with. An apparent technical fault should not lead to running scripts or pasting terminal code presented as a video-client update.

For people who suspect compromise, the bureau recommends securing cryptocurrency in a new crypto wallet created on an unaffected device, securing communication and developer accounts, alerting contacts and employers, and reporting to IC3 with the keyword FaceStealer. Alerting contacts can interrupt further approaches that could reuse the stolen account and recording.

#5143. The 7 Best Firming Body Lotions for Tightening Skin, Tested by Experts

Editors gave top marks to formulas from Nivea and Charlotte Tilbury.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Skin changes are part of life—thanks to sun exposure, the natural dip in collagen and elastin once you hit your late 20s, or shifts in weight (hi, pregnancy!). So if your skin doesn’t quite have the same snap-back it once did, that’s completely normal. The good news? You don’t need pricey lasers or an intense 10-step routine to see a difference. The right body-firming lotion can help skin look plumper, smoother, and more resilient.

Firming body lotions can offer smoother, tighter, and less dimpled skin. While nothing can compare to the results you may get from an in-office procedure—topicals aren’t going to work miracles, after all—you might be surprised at just how far hydration can improve the appearance of crepey skin. “The physical transformation of hydration can be profound on our skin,” says dermatologist Nava Greenfield, MD. “The skin will actually appear plumper when a lotion used to ‘firm’ is applied. Adding nutrients to the skin on a consistent basis can also help in creating a healthy, firm appearance.”

Like other categories of skincare products, some firming formulas will always be better than others. To help streamline your shopping experience, I asked dermatologists for their expertise on how to shop for body lotions, along with product recommendations.

For the past few months, beauty contributor Danielle Blundell and I have been researching and testing the best firming lotions. After consulting six dermatologists for their shopping guidance, we asked for their no-fail recommendations as a starting point. We got our hands on some of these picks and shared our testing feedback to help you determine which option works for your unique beauty needs. And to ensure there was a variety of firming body lotions across all budgets, we spent hundreds of hours vetting products for their ingredient list, formulation, absorbency, long- and short-term hydration and firming benefits, and pricing. Of the dozens we tested, these were the best ones we’re willing to auto-refill.

So, get ready for smoother, tighter, and, yes, firmer skin.

Given the fast-acting results Blundell experienced, and the impressive ingredient list we knew the Nivea Skin Toning Gel-Cream was our best overall option. When looking at price, packaging size, and the strength of a given formula’s ingredients, this lightweight cream is hard to beat.

The combination of antioxidant Coenzyme Q10, which aids in cell turnover, and L-carnitine, a chemical known to bolster skin energy reserves and oxygen consumption in skin cells, packs a firming and hydrating punch that’ll leave your skin feeling silky-smooth. We saw improved tightness in just two weeks with twice daily use, and you can choose between almond and lotus scents depending on your preferences for fragrances.

Blundell loves the gel-like texture of this one—it’s a little bit runny right out of the tube, but it sinks into her skin with minimal rubbing and goes on with a bit of a cooling sensation, which feels especially refreshing in the mornings before work and during any waterfront vacations you’re taking. Hours after a quick application (and even a SoulCycle class and quick shower later), Blundell’s legs looked slightly more taut and still felt supple to the touch, as though she had just put the lotion on.

Sometimes the best products are the ones you’ll use religiously. To that end, you can slather on this lotion morning, noon, and night, thanks to its under $10 price tag and light-but-creamy texture that’s easy to apply. Blundell saw results like immediate hydration, but it took three weeks to notice less crepey skin.

“Although the role of topical collagen isn't fully understood yet, this product contains a hydrating form of vitamin B3, niacinamide, and a form of B5 panthenol, which strengthen skin and improve skin quality,” says Dr. Nazarian. “It also absorbs really nicely and applies easily and quickly, making it a great and affordable option for improving skin health.”

Dr. Sartor mentions the lotion does include a nice mix of moisturizers (petrolatum, stearic acid) to prevent water loss as well as antioxidants (niacinamide, tocopheryl acetate) for firming benefits, especially for its cost. “It also contains free fatty acids (palmitic acid) to repair the skin barrier,” she adds.

The only downside for the price? The formula contains a synthetic fragrance, so if you have sensitive skin, you might want to skip it for that reason.

Why settle for just skin firming on your body when you enjoy it on your face as well? This 2-in-1 lotion earned major snaps from dermatologist Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, for that reason. "It has a powerful retinol and peptide complex that exfoliates to support the skin's renewal process," she says. That means it’ll go to work on discoloration and fine lines on your face and body while you sleep, since it’s a night treatment.

She highlights the intensive humectant and emollient moisturizers and vitamins that keep the skin hydrated for 24 hours as essential for skin firming and smoothing. You can see that in the texture; it’s rich and thick but still rubs in easily and dries quickly, so it’s not a pain to put on before bed.

A great place to give it a go first might be the neck and chest, where wrinkles tend to start popping up sooner than we all might like. Just keep in mind your skin type. Women with oily or combination skin might find it a tad heavy, so start with a pea-sized amount on the face and only add more as needed. Those with normal or dry skin will love this one due to its wonderfully hydrating formula.

Although Revision is a pricey pick, Dr. Nazarian argues it’s well worth the splurge because of the science-backed results and clinical trials. “It combines a cocktail of peptides and antioxidants to promote collagen, prevent breakdown, and ingredients like glucosamine to support cell turnover.” In other words, this product will help tighten loose skin.

BodiContour can be used before and after professional treatments to help enhance your results. However, you should wait until any broken skin is fully healed after your procedure before incorporating this cream back into your routine.

Dr. Sartor likes the hyaluronic acid in the formula as well but notes that the lotion is part of a three-step regimen. She thinks the brand’s promised results—from the fading of sun damage to the tightening of dimply, saggy skin—will be seen with use of the entire system. And even if a little lotion does go a long way, the instructions do recommend applying it twice a day and exfoliating twice a week. So with that does come a significant investment of time and money.

It's not called Magic Cream for nothing. This silky body cream blends caffeine and hydrating all-star hyaluronic acid to smooth and firm the skin. "It also includes the iconic magic 8 matrix, which includes vitamin C and E, aloe vera, camellia oil, rosehip oil, and shea butter, plus moisturizing frangipani flower extract," says dermatologist Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD. "Together this helps to brighten the skin and leave the skin glowing."

Of all the formulas Blundell tried, the Magic Body Cream is the one that left the most noticeable sheen and slight blurring effect on her skin. Putting it on feels luxurious, too; it’s rich but not so heavy that it doesn’t blend well, and it has a similar fragrance to its sister product, Magic Cream anti-aging face moisturizer. The only downside? At $65 a pop, it’s expensive, so Blundell saves it for nights when she’s showing a little skin or wants to target visible areas like the arms, legs, and tummy when sporting resort wear.

StriVectin is well regarded as a top-tier line for anti-aging and skin-firming products, and this rich body cream is a shining example of why the brand has a cult-like following among beauty insiders. And it all starts with the ingredients. A combination of turmeric root and jojoba seed extracts paired with a buttery blend of shea, murumuru, and cupuacu provide deep moisture to improve the look of skin texture and crepiness, says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. The turmeric helps brighten uneven skin tone while peptides and jojoba seed extract work together to tighten the skin and make it appear visibly more firm.

If you’re looking to fight back against particularly crepey arms or kneecaps, Dr. Sartor points out that this formula does include more antioxidants than some of the less expensive drugstore options. She also highlights the caffeine and collagen peptides, which work in tandem with the other firming extracts mentioned above. “This would be a good option for more mature skin in need of a richer moisturizer with more skin benefits,” she says.Although spending $44 might seem like a lot, there are other luxury anti-aging lotions out there selling for $165 to $220. If it helps, each container will last around 6 to 12 weeks, depending on how often you apply and if you’re slathering all over or just targeting a smaller area of your body. Regardless, even if you buy a few replacements in the year at $176, you get a year’s worth of product for significantly less than if you were splurging on a single high-end firming body lotion.

If you’re looking for an ultralight, gel-like product that can smooth, plump, and deliver silky-to-the-touch skin, then Nécessaire The Body Serum is the best pick for you. The formula is made with gentle clean ingredients that don’t skimp on quality. It combines ceramides with five molecular weights of hyaluronic acid which provides multilevel hydration. The result: a plumping finish that delivers a bit of lift and tautness. Glycerin further moisturizes the skin, while aloe vera calms redness and irritation. There’s also niacinamide for fine line-fighting benefits.

I’ve been using this serum on and off for a few years, and I can confidently attest to its effectiveness. It helps clear up eczema flare-ups, and has been a beauty lifesaver during the winter when it’s freezing outdoors and my radiator is cranked up inside. A single layer of the clear serum soaks into my skin in seconds, and if your skin is extra parched like mine is then you can apply additional layers as needed without pilling or leaving behind a sticky mess. It’s a year-round must-have for me because in the spring and summer I can just get away with using this instead of a thick lotion or cream.

“This serum does not have any firming ingredients but instead contains hyaluronic acid to plump skin appearance and ceramides to repair the skin barrier,” says Dr. Sartor. “This serum also contains lecithin to help prevent further water loss from the skin surface.”

Honestly, the only downside with this serum is that it’s fragrance-free. Nécessaire does fragrances so incredibly well that I wish they extended their enticing aromas into The Body Serum as well. Still, I fully stand by this serum and if you’re on the fence give it a go and see for yourself. With Amazon Prime’s signature two-day shipping and a 30-day money-back guarantee you have extra reassurance to treat yourself.

You’ve probably been using body lotion since middle school, and firming formulas look and feel roughly the same. They’re applied the same way, too; just massage a dollop into the skin, let it dry for a bit, and you’re good to go on with your day. A few key features, though, are what can separate a good option from a great one, and this is what you’ll want to consider when shopping for the best firming body lotions.

For dermatologist Dr. Rachel Nazarian, MD, certain ingredients are a must if you’re looking to tone and improve the skin’s texture.

Ultimately, whatever lotion, oil, serum, or cream you choose comes down to your skin’s needs. On the most basic level, sometimes it’s just a matter of texture preference—maybe you like the lightness of an oil or serum and want to go that route, or the richness of a cream is what you gravitate toward in the colder months. But some skin types really do fare better with certain formats over others, so you’ll want to keep that in mind.

Serums, gels, and lotions are lightweight and generally better suited for women under 40 with normal or acne-prone skin. Because they’re not heavy, they’re also fantastic if you have sensitive skin all over. You can follow it up with a cream as spot treatment in areas like your kneecaps and elbows that require more moisturization, says Dr. Sartor.

Creams are thick and deeply hydrating, making them helpful for dry and mature skin. You can also use them if you have sensitive skin. However, there is a trade-off. Hyaluronic acid penetrates the skin more easily in lighter serums and gels, so you might need to choose between a gentler product and a more effective moisturizer.

Though not as important as ingredients or format, size can matter when it comes to choosing a firming body lotion, mainly because it can factor into a product’s price and usage. If you want to make a smaller, more expensive lotion go further, consider applying it to target areas—think the butt, thighs, tummy, or upper arms. Consistency is key, though, so a product that you can use more frequently could be better than something you’d have to use sparingly.

Dr. Nava Greenfield, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City.

Dr. Rachel Nazarian MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist with Schweiger Dermatology Group in New York City.

Dr. Quynh-Giao Sartor, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist at Westlake Dermatology in Houston, Texas.

Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology: Medical Dermatology & Cosmetic Surgery in New York.

Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist and assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Cornell - New York Presbyterian Medical Center.

Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, FAAD, is a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology in New York.

It’s important to manage your expectations for firming lotions—they’re not the cure-all for sagging skin. Severe laxity and deep folds aren’t going to disappear overnight, but your skin will perk up and even plump a bit temporarily upon application.

“You can expect to see your skin slowly showing fewer fine lines and less sag,” says Dr. Greenfield. “A firming cream also has the potential to introduce nutrients that allow your skin to feel smoother and more supple.”

Proper timing is key for absorption and even application, so do yourself a favor and apply right after you’ve just bathed so it sinks in easily, especially if you’re only using this kind of product once a day.

“It is best to apply body lotion when your skin is still damp from a shower but not wet,” says Dr. Greenfield. “Towel dried is optimal. After exfoliating, it is crucial to apply a moisturizer. Best results will ultimately be with consistent and liberal use.”

“Creams are not capable of the same type of tightening that lasers and surgical options can offer,” says Dr. Nazarian. “Despite this, with consistent, continued use, you can certainly see improvement in laxity over time.” But again, commitment to regular use will impact results because everyone’s skin is fighting an uphill battle to a certain extent, at least when it comes to the loss of skin firmness and volume. For the best results, you have to commit to using one regularly to improve the quality of skin laxity, says Dr. Nazarian.

The short answer is yes—but with the caveat that it’s possible to have some kind of a reaction to any body lotion or cream. “Most of these body firming lotions have very little risk,” says Dr. Nazarian. “They are often directed to be used daily, some even twice a day. Major risks include irritation from one of the ingredients or a potential allergy to one of the ingredients.”

Just steer clear of anything with retinol in it, if you’re nursing or pregnant, and discontinue use of a product you have a negative reaction to. “Occasionally, people may experience drying of their skin, especially if the ingredients have the ability to decrease oil production, such as with retinol,” says Dr. Nazarian. “Monitor for those changes and decrease use if they are noted.”

Additional reporting by Danielle Blundell.

#5139. The 8 Best Gym Bags for Men, Tested by Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon, KNKG, and Mack Weldon came out on top in our testing.

NOT EVERY BACKPACK or duffel in my closet has what it takes to be a solid gym bag. I work out four times a week, and I’ve crammed sweaty clothes into work backpacks and tossed sneakers into flimsy totes, and they immediately smelled like a locker room. The truth is, hitting the gym is a gear-heavy activity, and if I’m going to stay consistent, I need a bag that does more than carry a water bottle and a stick of deodorant.

Because I live in New York City, when I’m heading to work out, I’m hauling office and performance clothes, shoes, headphones, and—more often than not—my work laptop too. A supermarket tote or random backpack just doesn’t cut it. To find gym bags suitable enough for our busy schedules, the Men’s Health team, including fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM, tested a bunch of different styles built for the job. The standouts are comfortable to carry, durable, spacious, and water-resistant to handle rainy commutes.

I narrowed it down to sleek, well-designed picks from brands like Dagne Dover, Lululemon, and Mack Weldon that move seamlessly from gym sessions to overnight trips. Most importantly, these gym bags keep things organized. Think separate compartments for sweaty workout shoes and gym shorts, odor-resistant linings, and smart pockets that prevent clean gear from mingling with the gnarly stuff. Because once you’ve experienced that cross-contamination, there’s no going back.

I've tested more than 30 different gym bags, but Lululemon's option blew the competition out of the water. I found it can transition from a duffle bag to a backpack by simply clipping the hidden straps onto the base of the bag, so I can wear it on my shoulders. It has a bunch of pockets to store a change of clothes, running shoes, jump ropes, water bottles, and more workout equipment.

Thanks to its water-repellent fabric that dries in seconds, my belongings didn't get soaked in rainy commutes. When this bag is not in use for the gym, it comes in handy for impromptu overnight stays and road trips, which means you can skip pulling out a bulky suitcase. And you can ensure that work gets done since there's a padded sleeve for your laptop.

The price may be a little steep, but we guarantee you can fit your entire life in this thing and get your money's worth. One more thing to know about this gym backpack is that its shoulder straps are very tough and made with nylon and elastane, which will not tear or fray a bit.

This gym bag has pockets galore: A total of 10 compartments will make organizing your gym clothes, fitness gear, and personal gadgets a breeze. We love that its shoe pocket is very spacious and fits up to men's size 14. In addition, it has its own wet pocket for storing wet towels, sweaty clothes, or swim trunks. There are two bottle holders as well, one for your pre-workout drink and another for your post-workout drink.

Based on our extensive testing, we found this bag is more than just reliable for the gym. Our gear editors have taken it for a spin during backcountry adventures and quick weekend excursions.

For those looking to declutter and uncomplicate their life, KNKG has made something really special with the Conquer duffel. Thorp likes that the organizing features of this bag are ingenious, giving you a pocket for every occasion, and I can effectively store anything from my laptop to my creatine for post-workout shakes.

In order to accomplish this, KNKG has designed easy-to-navigate dividers that you can change to fit your needs when it comes to compartments. These are not flimsy, which is what he’s come to expect after being burned by other brands. These are as solid as they get and will keep your running shoes or supplements in place.

Thorp is also a big fan of the KNKG Core backpacks, which are good for anyone who prefers to carry the load on their shoulders, but if you like the ability to change up how you carry, between handheld and over-the-shoulder, this is the way to go. Beyond what meets the eye, Dagne Dover’s carryall bag is designed to hold a great deal, last for a long time, and double as a stylish carry-on. Crafted from premium neoprene, it boasts a high-tech fabric that's super smooth and water-resistant to keep your gear dry on rainy days. Inside the main compartment, you'll find significant room for your typical gear as well as a shoe bag and dust bag to help prevent dirt or moisture from transferring to your clean duds. Plus, this section contains a dual water bottle slip pocket, so you’ll never be short on H2O at the gym or on a hike.

We’ve owned this bag for a few years, and the fabric’s tough structure has withstood the wear and tear better than the more expensive options out there. If it gets a scuff or a stain, you can pop it into the washer for easy cleaning. There's an adjustable shoulder strap to wear as a crossbody if you want to be hands-free. Not to mention, it's a sleek design that we don't mind showing off as we board flights, too.

You want to keep your dirty clothes away from your clean duds at all times.

#5136. XRP loans trigger 883 liquidations, and $53M remains at risk

Morpho liquidators seized 4.18 million cbXRP as XRP-backed borrowers repaid $4 million in debt, with $53.5 million still outstanding.

XRP-backed borrowers surrendered about 4.18 million cbXRP in 883 liquidation events on Morpho, as liquidators repaid just over 4 million USDC of debt.

The activity took place in a lending market on Base where borrowers pledge cbXRP to borrow USDC.

CryptoSlate's analysis of Morpho's indexed transaction records covers Nov. 7 at 10:30:51 UTC through Nov. 13 before 13:00 UTC. The 883 events count individual liquidation logs, so one person can be represented more than once.

A later snapshot on Nov. 13 still showed 53.53 million USDC outstanding.

An earlier loan-stress coverage used Nov. 6 positions to estimate that a further 10% oracle-price decline could bring 8.84 million USDC of debt across 1,070 positions to liquidation eligibility, assuming balances stayed unchanged.

The market's liquidation threshold is 62.5% loan-to-value, which compares the debt with the collateral's value: falling collateral prices can push the same loan above the permitted ratio.

Under Morpho's liquidation mechanism, an outside liquidator can repay some or all of an eligible position's debt and receive collateral plus an incentive. Here, that means paying USDC and taking cbXRP.

Collateral leaves the position while the debt obligation shrinks, and the records alone do not fully capture each borrower's economic outcome.

The largest daily repayment total in the selected window was about 1.58 million USDC on Nov. 8, followed by about 1.06 million on Nov. 10. All 883 selected liquidation records reported zero bad debt, the debt left uncovered by collateral.

The decoded liquidation log for a Nov. 10 transaction shows about 202,394 USDC repaid, and 218,175 cbXRP seized in the same market.

The liquidator then sent that cbXRP amount to another address and received USDC and wrapped ETH from that address in the same transaction. A separate Nov. 7 log records about 1,050 USDC repaid against 1,029 cbXRP seized.

Establishing native XRP selling would require evidence linking the seized collateral to subsequent XRP trading, including any redemption or custody movement along the way.

#5135. Robinhood’s Crypto Trading Volume Falls 48% in October as Event Contracts More Than Double

Crypto trading on Robinhood fell by almost half from a year ago in October, the company said Thursday, as customers traded $17 billion of digital assets while their bets on event contracts more than doubled.

The $17 billion figure was down 21% from September and 48% from October 2025, when crypto notional volume reached $32.5 billion. It covers both the flagship Robinhood app and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange the company bought in 2025.

Volume in the Robinhood app fell to $6.8 billion, down 24% from September and 51% from a year earlier. Bitstamp handled $10.2 billion, down 18% month over month and 45% year over year.

Average daily crypto volume across both platforms came to $548 million, compared with $713 million in September and about $1.05 billion a year ago. Daily average crypto trades slipped to about 700,000 from 900,000 in September and 1.1 million in October 2025.

The contrast with Robinhood’s prediction markets business is stark. Customers traded 5.9 billion event contracts in October, up 5% from September and 136% from the 2.5 billion traded a year earlier. Average daily volume reached 190 million contracts.

Robinhood counts crypto and prediction markets on the same 31-day calendar, since both trade every day, so the comparison is apples to apples. Event contracts let users bet on outcomes such as elections, sports and economic data, and October’s tally covered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

That growth has drawn scrutiny in Washington. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, plans to crack down on prediction markets and election betting platforms.

The rest of Robinhood’s brokerage held up better than crypto. Equity notional volume rose 2% from a year earlier to $325 billion, and options contracts traded climbed 8% to 289 million. Margin balances reached $22.9 billion, up 39% year over year.

Funded customers rose by about 130,000 in the month to 28.9 million, and net deposits came to $15.1 billion. Total platform assets slipped 3% from September to $383 billion but were up 12% from a year earlier.

Robinhood did not say why crypto activity fell. The release, like all of the company’s monthly updates, is unaudited and preliminary.

The slump in Robinhood’s crypto numbers lines up with a broader retreat by retail traders. Bitcoin ended September near $83,500 and has slid since, falling below $70,000 early Friday for the first time since August as a hot inflation report raised bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Institutional demand has cooled alongside it. U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday, and BlackRock’s IBIT, the largest of them, bled about $2 billion over nine sessions through Wednesday. Spot bitcoin ETFs have now erased their net inflows for 2026.

Crypto trading generates transaction revenue for Robinhood, so lower volume generally means fewer fees, even when assets on the platform keep growing. The company reports full fourth-quarter results early next year, and October’s figures are the first look at how the quarter started.

The company has kept expanding its crypto footprint anyway. In October, Robinhood won a license in Dubai to offer bitcoin and stock trading in the Middle East starting in 2027.

Robinhood also said cash and deposit balances fell 20% in October to $16.4 billion, mostly because customers were net buyers, and that the decline has largely reversed in early November. November’s operating data will show whether this month’s selloff below $70,000 brought crypto traders back or pushed more of them toward event contracts.

#5132. Urologists Have Some Hot Takes on Whether Men Should Sit or Stand to Pee

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AROUND THE WORLD—and on Reddit—there’s an eternal debate raging about whether men should sit or stand to pee. In the US, the answer seems like a no-brainer: standing. One YouGov poll found that only 10 percent of American men regularly sit down to pee, while 31 percent said they never do this. (There’s even that viral video years ago of a pastor arguing “a man is someone who pisses against the wall.”)

But that same YouGov poll found that where you wee varies. In Germany, 40 percent of guys actually sit down every time to urinate. About 22 percent of Swedish men, for example, sit down every time, but 28 percent sit down most of the time. Entire threads online are devoted to this question, including a hybrid tactic as a compromise in which a guy pees sitting down at home but stands up at a urinal in public.

Looking beyond preference, is there a right answer to take a leak? One study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics tried to give a definitive answer. Depending on your camp, the answer might validate what you know—or piss you off.

Researchers had no issue finding 52 guys to sign up for this peeing experiment. These dudes had no prior health issues and were between the ages of 18 and 39. The guys were randomly divided into two groups that sat to urinate. Then they would stand to pee. The other group did the same but in reverse order. Between each change in position was a "washout period" of 24 hours where guys did their business as usual.

Researchers tracked how much urine came out and how quickly. So who reigned supreme on the porcelain throne? Well, neither.

Sitting or standing to urinate didn’t change how much pee they got out in each session. There was a slight difference in how fast they got to max flow, though. Men were able to reach their peak speed slightly sooner when they peed sitting down, but researchers say this finding was “unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Meaning, one guy was pissing really hard while sitting, while everyone else peed at a similar rate and volume no matter what position they did it.

The findings are not surprising to S. Adam Ramin, MD, urologist and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists. “If you're a normal, young, healthy male, it will make no difference whether you sit or stand to urinate,” he says. “You will have a good stream either way.”

THE FINDINGS WOULD likely be different for older men, especially those with an enlarged prostate. “Sometimes in older men with an obstructing prostate, sitting to urinate may help them to empty their bladders more effectively as they are able to generate more abdominal force to squeeze the urine out,” says Boback Berookhim, MD, urologist at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital.

HEALTHWISE, NOT REALLY. But if you have a certain preference for one over the other, then there’s no harm in sticking with one position. There's some convenience with standing to pee: You pull it out, do your business, and move on. Peeing this way is “likely to save time,” says Dr. Berookhim.

Sitters, on the other hand, might prefer the position because it’s slightly more hygienic. Dr. Ramin says guys are more likely to splash, sprinkle on the toilet seat, or even miss entirely when they’re standing versus sitting. Plus, sitters might be more likely to wash their hands after every use. Men are 1.5 times less likely to wash their hands than women after peeing—probably where they could use those saved seconds.

Beyond that necessary bathroom etiquette, there’s really no other reason to switch up your tried-and-true urinary habits. Dr. Berookhim says he certainly wouldn’t tell a young, healthy guy to change the way they are using the bathroom if they are already doing fine.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#5130. Diesel prices plunge 8%, yet Bitcoin traders face a squeeze

October’s PPI slowed at the headline level, but higher freight prices and firm underlying inflation leave financing relief uncertain.

US wholesale inflation slowed in October, but rising freight prices and firm underlying pressure complicate the case that cheaper fuel will make financing easier for Bitcoin (BTC) holders while BTC remains below $70,000.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ October producer-price report, released Nov. 13, showed diesel prices falling 7.9% as truck freight prices rose 3.9%. Headline wholesale inflation slowed sharply, but the measure excluding food, energy, and trade services kept rising at September’s monthly pace.

Final-demand PPI rose 0.3% in October, seasonally adjusted, after September’s revised 1.4% increase.

The measure excluding food, energy and trade services rose 0.5% for a second month. Its annual increase eased to 4.9% from 5%, while headline annual PPI accelerated to 6.5% from 6.3%. Those readings support a mixed assessment of some comparisons improved, but underlying monthly pressure held firm.

BLS attributed more than 80% of October’s 0.2% rise in final-demand services prices to truck freight. Transportation and warehousing services rose 2%, even as final-demand energy prices slipped 0.1%. Goods prices increased 0.5%.

Cheaper diesel coexisted with higher prices for moving goods. For now, the freight increase undercuts an assumption that a lower fuel bill immediately means cheaper transport.

Unprocessed intermediate goods prices fell 3.1%. Alongside slower monthly headline inflation and the easing annual exclusion measure, that gives the more optimistic interpretation real evidence. The question is whether that cooling broadens and lasts.

Diesel and truck freight moved in opposite directions in October. The inflation picture also changes with the comparison window.

September → October 2026: headline PPI slowed; the measure excluding food, energy and trade services stayed at 0.5%.

September → October 2026: annual headline PPI rose from 6.3% to 6.5%; the exclusion measure eased from 5.0% to 4.9%.

Fuel relief coexists with firm underlying monthly inflation; annual readings are mixed.

PPI series describe different producer prices. Concurrent diesel and freight changes do not establish cause or pass-through timing. Monthly changes are seasonally adjusted; annual changes are unadjusted. PPI is distinct from CPI and PCE.

PPI measures the selling prices domestic producers receive, CPI measures prices paid by consumers, while the Fed targets inflation measured by personal consumption expenditures (PCE).

The measures overlap in the economic pressures they describe, but their readings are not interchangeable.

Speaking before that day’s CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller leaned toward further tightening through a 25-basis-point December rate increase if conditions developed as expected.

He said a 50-basis-point increase should be considered if October core CPI resembled the previous two readings around 0.3% or higher.

The subsequent CPI report showed a 0.4% monthly headline increase and a third consecutive 0.3% increase excluding food and energy.

The Fed’s explanation of monetary policy describes how policy-rate changes affect short-term interest rates and broader financial conditions. Applied to Bitcoin, the conditional mechanism is that lower financing costs could make borrowed exposure easier to carry, while easier conditions could encourage investors to allocate more to risk.

The route from producer prices to financing relief remains conditional. Persistent inflation could keep policy restrictive even when one fuel price falls, while a recovery case based on financing relief needs evidence beyond cheaper diesel.

Farside Investors' completed Nov. 12 row records US Bitcoin ETF net outflows of $284.1 million, preceding the PPI release.

ETF flows describe one investment channel. Still, completed inflows would provide firmer evidence of buyers returning than an inflation-based expectation alone.

Broader cooling in consumer and producer prices, less restrictive assessments from policymakers and observable financing relief would strengthen the case that fuel declines are becoming useful for Bitcoin holders.

Sustained ETF inflows would add demand evidence, while continued underlying inflation pressure and further withdrawals would keep that case weaker, even if diesel keeps getting cheaper.

#5128. This Popular Supplement May Also Be the Key Behind Healthier Knees

You’re probably not getting enough of it, either.

Knee osteoarthritis can be a debilitating condition due to the joint pain, stiffness, and swelling it causes. Unfortunately, it's a reality for an estimated 14 million Americans. There are a range of potential treatment options that can help, including cortisone shots and GLP-1s, but a new study suggests a more accessible option may also help: taking a fiber supplement.

Research from a recent clinical trial published in the journal Nutrients suggests that adding a daily fiber supplement could ease pain from knee osteoarthritis, strengthen your muscles, and maybe even make you feel pain less intensely.

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends having 14 grams of fiber for every 1,000 calories you consume, which means most women should aim for 25 grams of fiber daily, while men should strive for 38 grams each day. But the average American only eats around 17 grams of fiber per day, suggesting that many of us consistently fall short on this important nutrient.

Experts aren’t saying that you should take a fiber supplement instead of physical therapy or seeing a specialist for knee pain. But if you're doing everything else right, adding a fiber supplement to your routine might be worth trying out. Here's why.

Meet the experts: Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher in the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham; Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology; Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California

For the study, researchers recruited 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis and split them into four groups. One group took a 20-gram daily inulin supplement (inulin is a naturally occurring fiber that's considered a prebiotic—it’s also commonly found in healthier soda alternatives), another did digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE), the third group did a combination of inulin and physical therapy, and the final group took a placebo.

Researchers discovered that people in the inulin and PT groups had less knee pain, and that people who took inulin had other perks that didn't surface in the physical therapy group, like better grip strength and less pain sensitivity. Also worth noting: Those who took inulin were more likely to stick with their prescribed treatment compared to the 21 percent of people in the PT-only group who dropped out.

“Earlier studies had linked certain gut bacteria, such as Streptococcus, to worse knee pain,” says Afroditi Kouraki, lead study author and researcher at the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham. That, plus feedback from people suffering from knee arthritis who said they wanted diet-based ways to manage their pain, led Kouraki and her team to study inulin.

The researchers didn't study the why behind this association, but experts have a few theories. "Good gut bacteria feed on fiber like inulin and, in doing so, they produce substances that calm inflammation and help keep the gut lining healthy," Kouraki says. Your gut "talks" to your brain and nerves, and it can influence how sensitive you are to pain, she explains.

Kouraki points out that people in the study who took inulin also had higher levels of the gut hormone GLP-1 (yep, that GLP-1), which is also tied to pain regulation, and that those with bigger rises in GLP-1 tended to have a stronger grip. "These clues are early, and we need more research to understand exactly what’s going on," she says.

But it's important to put the findings into context. "Exercise still did more to improve walking and chair-rise ability, which matters for patients," says Timothy Gibson, MD, orthopedic surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Joint Replacement Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

And while the findings suggested perks with taking an inulin supplement, they weren't huge differences, points out Will Harvey, MD, rheumatologist at Tufts Medical Center and president of the American College of Rheumatology. "At best, further study is warranted," he says.

People concerned about their joints will often take collagen, glucosamine and/or chondroitin. But "there is no strong evidence to support the use of dietary supplements," Dr. Harvey says.

Kouraki also points out that collagen and glucosamine are aimed at the joint itself, while inulin works indirectly through the gut bacteria and the body’s immune and hormone systems. "It’s a different approach, using diet and the gut to help manage symptoms,” she says.

Knee pain is complicated, and it's a stretch to say that taking a fiber supplement will make everything better. "This doesn’t replace proven treatments like exercise and physiotherapy, which also worked well in our study," Kouraki says. "But it suggests diet could be a useful extra tool."

And, of course, if you're in pain and it's not getting better, talk to your doctor. They should be able to suggest alternative strategies to make you more comfortable.

#5127. FutureBit’s Apollo III Bitcoin Miner Hits Micro Center Shelves in Its First Brick-and-Mortar Launch

FutureBit is putting its Apollo III Full Node on sale Friday at four Micro Center stores, the first time customers can walk into a shop and take home one of the Brooklyn company’s bitcoin miners.

The compact home miner, which also runs a full bitcoin node, will be sold in Brooklyn, Miami, Tustin, California, and Austin, Texas, as those stores open Friday, FutureBit said in a release. The four-store launch coincides with the grand opening of Micro Center’s new Austin store, the chain’s 31st U.S. location and its third in Texas.

Customers will also be able to reserve a unit online for in-store pickup, the company said. It did not say how many units each store has in stock, or what Micro Center is charging for them.

Until now, buyers in North America had to order the machine from FutureBit’s website, where the company says units are in stock and ship in two to three days. Putting it on a computer-store shelf lets a customer look at the hardware, ask how it works and carry it out the same day.

“When we started FutureBit, we made weekly trips to the DIY electronics section at the Brooklyn Micro Center to buy parts,” said John Stefanopoulos, founder of FutureBit. “On Friday, someone can walk into that same store, ask how Bitcoin mining works and take home a miner we designed just down the street. We couldn’t be more excited to work with Micro Center on our first physical store launch.”

FutureBit’s own shop lists the Apollo III Full Node at $1,099.99 without a storage drive, $1,299.99 with 1 terabyte of SSD storage and $1,399.99 with 2 terabytes. A cheaper, miner-only “Standard” model starts at $899.99 but does not include the full node.

The Full Node is rated at up to 18 terahashes per second in Turbo mode, at about 325 watts. In Eco mode, it is listed at about 12 TH/s and 150 watts, with noise under 35 decibels. A Super Eco mode is listed at about 8 TH/s and 80 watts. Power can be adjusted from 50 to 400 watts, and Turbo mode is much louder, at about 55 decibels. Those power figures are measured at the board and can vary by 10%, the product page says.

The unit is a 6.5-by-6.5-by-6-inch cube that weighs 6.5 pounds, comes with a one-year limited warranty and is assembled in the United States. It uses new 3-nanometer, American-designed chips, a custom controller and 8 GB of memory, and it includes a built-in solo mining pool. Buyers can also point the miner at a standard bitcoin mining pool. FutureBit says the full node and solo-mining features require an SSD, which is not included in the $1,099.99 configuration.

Bitcoin Magazine covered the Apollo III’s debut in February, when FutureBit introduced the hardware as a way for individuals to run both a miner and a node at home. The point, the company has long argued, is not to compete with industrial mines on cost.

A single Apollo III at 18 TH/s is a sliver of the bitcoin network. A home-scale setup in that range still faces expected times to a solo block measured in centuries at recent difficulty, Bitcoin Magazine previously noted. Even so, a miner running through FutureBit’s Apollo Solo setup found block 973,262 on Oct. 26 and collected the full 3.154 bitcoin reward.

FutureBit, based in Brooklyn, has built consumer mining hardware since 2015. Stefanopoulos has framed store shelves as a way to put more hash rate and more nodes in living rooms. The company did not say whether the Micro Center test will expand beyond the four stores that began selling the Apollo III on Friday.

#5124. Not Ready For a Facelift? No Problem: Welcome to The Era of “In-Between” Treatments.

No surgery, minimal downtime, a firmer, more lifted look—what’s not to love?

THE RISE OF BUZZY noninvasive in-office treatments is no coincidence. These days, people want to look sculpted, lifted, and more refreshed without having to make the somewhat uneasy decision to go under the knife. And as more and more patients seek meaningful results without committing to surgery, there’s a growing interest in treatments that bridge the gap between injectables and a facelift, aptly dubbed the “in-between” treatments.

These interventions will still give you meaningful lifting, volumizing, sculpting, and tightening results without as much downtime (sometimes, none at all) or diminishing returns on your investment. Think of them as the individualized, targeted treatments you can utilize before considering a face or neck lift. The trick is having a solid understanding of what specific technologies can—and cannot—accomplish. If you’re not pairing the right treatment with the right concern, you’re shelling out good money to “correct something it fundamentally cannot address,” explains Connie Yang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City.

Filler, for instance, is effective for restoring strategic areas of volume loss on the face, but it can’t truly lift tissue or remove excess skin. “If you add more filler in an attempt to recreate a sharper jawline or lift the lower face, you’re just going to end up making the face look heavier and puffier, rather than more lifted and sculpted,” says Dr. Yang.

Meet the experts: Connie Yang, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. Jennifer Levine, MD, is a double board-certified facial plastic surgeon in New York City.

In a similar vein to filler, energy-based skin devices such as radio frequency (think: Morpheus 8 or Xerf) or ultrasound devices such as Ultherapy that target the deeper, structural layers of the face can only do so much up to a certain point. “These treatments can give meaningful improvement in the right patient, but there’s a limit to how much contraction you can achieve non-surgically,” says Dr. Yang. If someone has significant jowling, excess skin, or deeper tissue descent, repeated treatment with these types of devices will end up giving someone only progressively smaller improvements over time.

To give you the LD on all of your options, we spoke with experts about what each treatment can realistically accomplish, what patients can expect over time results-wise, and when you should skip straight to surgery.

As a rule of thumb, most (not all) aesthetic professionals will generally advise you to exhaust all options before spending a pretty penny on a facelift. In the end, it’s an individual decision. Either way, in-office treatments can help to keep your skin radiant and build collagen to help you to get an even better result for when it is time for a facelift. Think about throwing a crumpled up sheet over your mattress in the morning: If you don’t iron it first, the wrinkles will still be there when you go to make the bed.

There's no one-size-fits-all approach because not all facial aging is the same. For patients that are truly getting closer to being surgical candidates, “focusing on improving skin quality and some degree of skin tightening can be your best bet, while at the same time managing expectations of the limitations of devices and their expected outcomes,” says Dr. Yang.

Double board-certified facial plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine, MD, who uses a combination of injectable treatments and non-surgical devices in addition to surgery in her practice, recommends treatment protocols depending on which components of aging are most responsible for the patient’s concerns.

The following treatment categories are considered the in-betweeners that you may want to consider before going under the knife.

“This is an important option for select patients with earlier skin laxity who want gradual tightening and a degree of lifting,” says Dr. Levine. Ultrasound imaging allows providers to actually visualize tissue layers and guide energy placement.

It’s FDA-cleared for use to lift the brows and help with lax tissue beneath the chin and neck—the places where aging skin can be most obvious. “I consider it an in-between treatment because it can address laxity through targeted tissue remodeling while the patient’s expectations remain appropriate for a nonsurgical result,” says Dr. Yang, but “[they do] not replicate the degree of lifting you can achieve surgically.”

These work best when texture, dermal remodeling, and modest tightening are the goals. Dr. Levine says that for these treatments, energy settings and treatment depth play a huge role and must be chosen carefully based on anatomy. RF microneedling is provider-dependent, especially because at the wrong setting, facial fat loss, unintended scarring, and nerve injury can occur.

“I consider this particularly valuable when fine lines, uneven pigmentation, and textural changes contribute substantially to an aged appearance,” explains Dr. Levine. Improving the skin’s surface can make a meaningful aesthetic difference, especially for someone who is beginning to develop skin laxity. She points out that “improvement in skin quality is a different endpoint from repositioning descended facial tissue.”

Ellacor is the best example of a true in-between option, says Dr. Yang, “because it actually removes microscopic cores of skin without surgery, allowing the skin to contract as it heals.” Instead of just heating the skin to stimulate collagen, it uses tiny hollow needles to physically remove microscopic columns of excess skin, scarlessly. As the skin heals, it contracts and remodels, which can help to improve wrinkles and laxity.

Patient selection for this treatment is especially important because there is some downtime involved and a risk of pigment change. That said, it’s useful for those with mild to moderate laxity and early jowling, who don’t quite have enough excess skin or tissue to warrant a facelift yet.

Brand Names: Sculptra, Radiesse, Juvederm, Restylane

When true volume deficiency contributes to someone’s overall concern, Dr. Levine says that conservative volume restoration with the use of hyaluronic acid fillers or biostimulatory injectables that boost skin’s own collagen production can help to improve contours and balance the face.

Let’s just get this out of the way right off the bat—age alone isn’t the biggest determining factor in whether or not someone would benefit from a facelift. Genetics, lifestyle choices, and how someone cares for their body and skin have a huge impact. “I have patients in their 40s with very little laxity who are excellent candidates for non-invasive treatments and younger patients whose anatomy or degree of tissue descent make certain treatments less effective,” explains Yang.

And while there’s no single telltale sign to know when it’s time for a facelift, one of the main factors is whether the patient has “skin laxity alone or true tissue descent that requires surgical repositioning,” says Dr. Yang. With skin laxity, the skin can appear creepy or loose with decreased elasticity and can be pinched more easily. “Tissue descent is a deeper structural change; if you manually reposition the deeper tissue upward and it significantly restores the contours of the cheek or jawline, that tells me that the concern isn’t just loose skin and that a facelift would be the solution,” explains Dr. Yang.

Even if someone is a candidate for a non-invasive treatment, if they're ultimately looking for a dramatic lift or significant change in their facial contours, then surgery may be the answer. Dr. Yang says that she is more inclined to recommend surgery after a patient has gone through multiple rounds of injectables or tightening treatments and they continue to chase the same concern with diminishing improvement or returns. “At that point, continuing to add filler or repeatedly treating with devices can become costly without addressing the underlying structural issue,” she says.

Before diving face first into a surgery, Dr. Yang encourages her own patients to really explore all of their options and think deeply about their long-term goals. If you know that a facelift is in your future, it may shape what is recommended to you by a provider. “I don’t want you spending years of over-treating or investing in procedures that may only give you marginal improvement.” Instead, she says, the focus should be on maintaining skin quality and aging well until you’re ready. Conversely, if you’re unsure whether surgery will ever be an option for you, finding the right provider to work with can help you to maximize non-surgical options available in order to get the most meaningful results possible.

Overall, the goal should be to maximize what you have and age well, while recognizing when you’ve reached the limitations of non-surgical treatments. “If surgery may eventually be the right choice, you want to arrive there with healthy, well-maintained skin,” she says. Amen to that.

#5123. Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

Crypto hackers stole $8.7 billion so far in 2026, surpassing the projected annual onchain revenue generated across the industry, according to ARK’s research director.

Hackers stole 57 cents for every $1 earned onchain by blockchain protocols since 2017, according to Lorenzo Valente, director of digital asset research at ARK Investment Management.

“Security is the bottleneck,” wrote Valente in a Thursday X post, sharing a chart showing that $8.7 billion lost to crypto hacks year to date had already surpassed the $5.6 billion in estimated annual onchain revenue for 2026.

Since 2017, the crypto industry has lost about $26.9 billion to hacks and earned $47 billion in total onchain revenue, he added.

The recent $6.3 billion stolen in the Binance hack alone exceeded Valente’s estimate for full-year 2026 onchain revenue. Value lost to hacks is on track to exceed onchain revenue by year-end for the first time since 2020.

The crypto industry saw a string of high-value hacks this year, including September’s $387 million Bitget hack and the $320 million Liquid Network exploit, as well as April’s $295 million Drift Protocol exploit.

The mounting security exploits are weighing on the institutional appetite for DeFi. In an April research note, JPMorgan analysts identified bridge security as a long-standing challenge for the industry.

Total value locked in decentralized finance (DeFi) has fallen nearly 10% since the Binance exploit, from $85.9 billion on Oct. 29 to $77.4 billion on Thursday, according to DefiLlama.

#5120. Louisiana sues Kalshi, Robinhood and other prediction markets in escalating regulatory fight

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill said she filed a lawsuit against platforms Kalshi, Robinhood, Polymarket, Forecastex, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Novig, Underdog, Gemini and Prophetx.

Louisiana is the latest state to take on prediction market platforms, joining a growing legal battle between states and the federal government over who has jurisdiction to regulate the industry.

On Thursday, Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill said she filed a lawsuit against platforms Kalshi, Robinhood, Polymarket, Forecastex, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Novig, Underdog, Gemini and Prophetx for breaking the law.

"For too long, they have violated our laws with impunity," Murrill said in a post on X. "No longer: I am seeking an immediate restraining order and an injunction to restore the rule of law in Louisiana."

Louisiana is now the 11th state to sue one or more prediction markets following Arkansas, Utah and Connecticut, among others. And platforms have fired back. Following the lawsuit on Thursday, Kalshi filed an emergency temporary restraining order in preparation.

"Based on recent discussions with representatives of the state of Louisiana, Kalshi believes that the State will initiate an action against Kalshi in state court to restrict Kalshi from operating in Louisiana," Kalshi said in its court filing.

Prediction markets became massively popular following the 2024 presidential elections, with some of the biggest platforms now worth billions of dollars. States have generally taken issue specifically with sports betting and say that platforms are operating illegally and are avoiding paying taxes. The issue also brings up concerns among tribal organizations about how the platforms could circumvent agreements.

Meanwhile, platforms have argued that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission should be in charge of regulating the platforms, including sports betting. The CFTC has also sued states to get "exclusive jurisdiction," which could later make its way up to the Supreme Court.

On Thursday, a Robinhood spokesperson asserted that its event contracts are federally regulated by the CFTC in response to Louisiana's lawsuit.

"As we've previously shared, Robinhood's event contracts are federally regulated by the CFTC and offered through Robinhood Derivatives, LLC, a CFTC-registered entity, allowing retail customers to access prediction markets in a safe, compliant, and regulated manner," the spokesperson told The Block.

A Coinbase spokesperson called states' approach fragmented.

"Louisiana's lawsuit, filed while multiple federal appellate courts actively consider the same issues, is another example of the fragmented enforcement Congress sought to prevent when it gave the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

The Coalition for Prediction Markets, which represents several of the platforms sued on Thursday, said the lawsuit was "troubling and unlawful."

"Louisiana’s attack on this industry is a troubling and unlawful attempt to assert state authority over markets governed by federal law that would only cut off people’s access to an important tool for gathering market information, expressing informed views, and hedging risks based on their own expertise," that spokesperson said. "That cannot stand."

Separately, CNBC reported on Wednesday that the CFTC is investigating whether Kalshi failed to inform the CFTC properly about its proposed event contracts.  This comes soon after Reuters reported that the CFTC is investigating Polymarket over whether it violated a deal made in 2022 to promise to ban U.S. users from its flagship overseas platform.
